div.head: LADIES' LETTER. \
div.p: LADIES' LETTER. \

MY DEAR NELLI* No species of head4gear is more comfortable in the train than a fur cap, but for short journeys a pliant felt hat with the simplest trimmings, a sash of bird's-eye surah threaded through a buckle smartened by a couple of quills, is very pretty and effective. For hats, transparent crinoline straw is much used, and some very charming models in black crinoline, run with chenille, have waved brims and low crowns and are trimmed with chau bows of black tulle and clusters of white roses with jet centres. Other pretty hats are of fine black chip or satin straw, with broad brims drooping slightly back and front, and a trimming of sweeping black ostrich feathers, lo)ps of soft satin ribbon and clusters of shaded purple violets. Toques continue to be large and rather flat and n.re frequently made of tucked mauve or amethyst silk, relieved by a few deeper purple auriculas or violets, or a couple of big rosettes of white tulle. Tucked white cloth is another popular material for toques, while not a few are of very open fancy black straw run through with velvet baby-ribbon.

appears that all _ now are printed with a double pattern—that is to say, on a white background there is a white pattern, over-printed with one or two different designs in tolack. The prettiest of these are those which have a flowery or conventional pattern mingled with one of lacy effect. One of the most charming materials for evening wear bears the poetical name of the Vole lactee, or the Milky Way, in rich white silk, shot with can.. stellation of gold or silver stars, suppoe'j to be suggestive of the starry path in the hinvens. For older women the satin soutac44 ts a handsome fabric for trains and panals is printed with a fl dark background 2313'.7 n.ttern in rich colourings, outlined with a.sta . thmad. It 1-.oerto tcn in gold or silver a adaptation of the cretonne applique on clots-which has been so falhionable all the what9T. OPl'.y t hat this is all in satin.

i ways a little difficuil, , choose dresses for girls of 15 or so. They should not be too elaborate, and yet an utter simplicity cannot be recommended. The awkwardness inseparable from fast-growing young creatures who have not yet attained per- fect cornmaaa over their limbs is made still more trying by a plain skirt. A flounce on the cloth costnme removes this disadvantage, and yet adds nothing serious in the way of weight to the dress. The trimmings are machine-stitchiugs only, a few rows bordering the flounce, a few more heading it, others hiding the seams. The little bolero is in the cloth, with a black silk collar ornamented with several rows of stitching. The black silk skirt has a stitched front, and the spotted tie is also stitched.

Those who bought black and white or mauve hats in haste have repented at leisure, for the preseflt. mourning does not admit of anything but an all- black hat. These have been, and will continue to be, probably right on through the year, exceedingly S. la mode, especially the toquet kind, of swathed tulle, mousseline, or crushed crin, awl also the large picture typo of hat. Chiffon and silk roses, black violets, or cowslips are favourite flowers, and skeletionised leaves and wings are very pretty, traced, outlined, and spangled with powdered jet.' Many of the lat izer hats and toques are furnished with soft, wido tulle strings, coming from behind and tied under the chin or on the left side in a huge bow ; these have a softening effect to the face. Very long oblong clasps and buckles are features on most of the hats.

A nice black beaver hat was sharply up-turned at the sides and there trimmed with hea7y puffs of black panue starting from bright jet bosses above the softly puffed- coiffure. A jet buckle threaded through a scarf of panne is passed round the brim, which at the back dip., upon tho knotted chignon. Several of the milliners are trimming their toques no longer up the front, but are depend- ing upon widely spreading brims made of folds of silk, buckled at the sides with jet, for their effect above the brow, and at the back a how half rest- ing upon the hsir, half raised on high. Jet strips like ribbon brighten some of the new mourni,ig millinery, wound bee-hive fashion round the shape. Your loving JRNZTIE.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

There is a gond deal of banter on the 'subject of Scottish bagpipes, proceeding often from people whe not stop to ask themselves whether they like the pipee I or not. The Saslten of Morocco, on the other hand, is said to be" deeply fascinated " with Highland music, and net only keeps a Court piper, but has ordered a see for his own use. There seems to be an oppartunity for some enterprising Irishman t) obtain, from hes swarthy Majesty,an advertisement for the Irish bagpipes, which are said by the prole of Ireland to be sweeter ;.:taan those of Scotland, but are sildom heard beyond the shores of Ecin. Much disappointment will be caused in Glasprow by the inability of the Kng to open ite'ereat lacer natienat Exhibition in May. Owing to the Co art beine in full mourning, his Majesty has reluctantly been cm,elled to abandon the engagement, and it is expected that the Duchess of Fife wrll new preside at the opening cere- mony. The Exhibition, which promisee to be a great success,will no doubt attract many visitors to Scetleed, during the holiday season, not onle from other parts of the country, but also from abroad. The King and Queen will certainly visit Glasgow later on in the year, in all probability when their Majnities go to Balmoral in the autumn. There does not appear to be any cause for the dis- quieting rumours as to the King's health, which have lately been current on the Continent. His If sjasty has bad much to try him lately, and what with State aff airs I and personal gtief, it would Ecsrcely b surprisiug it the I King showed some evidence of the strain that hes been ut upon him. It is perfectly obvious that the arrange- ments for the departure of the Duke and Duchess ot Cornwall and York would not have been allowed to pro- ceed if there was the slightest truth in the Contineatal rumours of the King's impaired cendition. Some colour is perhaps lent to these en esseetiens by the fact that the L:fe Aesurance offiees are asking more than the usual terms for policies on the King's life. It is not an uncommon thing for peep'e to insure the life of the Severeeen, and there are many huaineseo ntrac's leases, and the Ilk-, which are closely interwoven with the demise of the Crown, and which are peon cnsd by assurance. In the case of King E lward, the premiuma are high, usually being the same es for hots seesral years more adyancee than his Majesty's It hewenn- dues net follow that the high premiums ere induced by considerations of health or constitutim, as in any offices hive declined to take the lives of Severeigensince the assassinations of the late King of Rely and the .Empress of Austria. The Countess of Limerick's Shamrock League is organising the distributinn of little bunches of genuine green ;for St. Patrick'a Day—the 17th of March taT ne this year en a Sunday. Twelve months ago, the kindly action of Queen Victoria aroused an interest in St. Patrick's Day which extended far beyond the Emerald Isle. Not only in the Mother Country. but throughout the Empire, it was made the general o-caaion for hommr- ing the conspicuous bravery of the Irish regiments. There is now an opportunity for perpetuating this memory, and at the same time displayMe a little patriotism, by purchasing boxes of the .bartroth which the Countess of Limerick is cfn ring at 23 61 and 4- 61, for the basalt of the funds of the Majors' and Sailers' Families Association. Ireland's national emblem has given rise to endless dis- cussions, as to what is the genuine shamrock, as also with regard to the use made ef the "triune symb "by St. Patrick. leenr used to be a legend that the sham- tnck grew nowhere but in Ireland, but it may be tourist just as easily in Britain, en in France. To' Lish them- selves have had thsir differences whether the g noire green is what is commonly lc-teem as the wale-lessee or white clover, or the yellow trefoil, bet it does nut much matter, at least t 3 anyone who ie not Itch, sense every trefoil plant will do for the purpose to which St. Patriek is supposed to have put it, the illustration of the Trinity. /deny reasons have also b 'en assigned for the Welsh custom of wearing leek or St. David's Day, the let of March, just the same as there is much uncertainty about the famous Order of the Garter. The most nem:- lar version of the Welsh custom is, that St. D avid advised the Minns to wear a leek In their caps, to dis- tinguish friends from f ) sin their battles with tl2e Saxocs. There is a little doubt that the Garter had its origin in the same idea, though there are several other plausible and inconsequent versions of ite originality. When battles consisted of band to han I cleft as, it was not only necessary to distinguish friends trim fees, but the bravest were hidden to wear a oistinctive mark, such as a garter tied round the leg, which distinguished them as leader?, and hence the h ,nour at' ached to the ! symbol. The general transformation from dead Week to half- mourning co:numbers affected • brightness in the streets and shops which is a great relief to the sombre aspset things during the past few wet ki, Snare people there are, who have practically gone out of mournine, and this is especially the case with Roman Catholics, who are not unnaturally e ffended at the religious intolerance displayed towards them in the formal deeatetione from the Throne, but the great mejerity will wait until July, before donning any hut ha'r-mourning tints. Regarding the mauves, now beine ehewa so extensively, the blusr shades should be carefully avAded, as these are far from becoming to the bet complexions, aeid particularly treinn to indifferent cries. London in Lent le always dull, and this year it is duller than usual. Pew have remeiaed in ;town ri isnu'd leave it, and numbers of lttncietr folk are abroad, whore they will remain for some tires to Coma. Travel- ling toilettes have been receiving careful attention oF late, and there is litt e doubt that we now trtv-i much Imore artistically than wat once our e °et the new emi-fitting ceats are delightful. For the train, the best am mg them ate of silk or sloth,. I and cinder grey in colour, a hue that wears we:t,, and shows no trace of Just. For steamboat wear, the ooat is Usually of fri,ze,of like colour,and this is- accornlanied hy a pliant felt tine with the 3impirisb of trimmings— just a ribbon b.ind and a• couple of quills.. for , prnforecce. The mixed materials that are nosv to be haeleare ti prove a boon and a blessing to those to whom I the British climate at this particular season proves-aeme- I what trying. le duty silk-faced fabrial are much in ' evidence, for evening bleuses, and none but those "in the know" would suspect that they possess a woollen back. Then there are the cottoe-faced arerials, whioh aiso possess a back of wool. Hitherto it has been quite late in the spring 'ere the majority of us could•veatu re ; to don our cotton shirts without fearing a.cold or chi 11,1 but all this is altered now. By cyclists these new fabrics are lik<ly to be much appreciated, a little later on. Steel premises to enjoy a wide vogue this spring and coming summer. Beautiful embroideries- are being shown, and on black gowns these look particularly well. Many hlack teques show a treeing of steel, and, black silk rufli s, with the eders- sewn with loops of cue steel beads, are among the n,,velties of the moment. Steel err amente, once so fashionable, are well to the fore again, but about all this there is one great disadvantage, —the care that is needed to protect both trimmiegs and ornaments from damp. , The time is drawing near for that yearly earthquake spring cleaning." Th some householos tt is got through already, but tor comfort, the raiddle ef April is quite earl.: enotteh to set one's house,in ordei for the summer. Floors and woodwork take much longer to dry when the weather is chilly and unsettled, and the ta kof cleaning down is more of a burden than when the bright mild ,fisys have arrived. Moreover it is very depressing to have to sic fieeless, and perchance alm sst freeze, just because • 'the chimneys have been swept " and fresh hangings put up. The spring cleaning is a ' very necessary procedure if our well-being is to be cm n- siderei, but it is surely wise to chose a suitable time and opportunity for the upheaval. " MADG E.

div.p: CHAPTER XX . AN ULTIMATUM.
Tis a bold game to play, Yet I:must risk it."

['After -the visit of 111 r. Bice there was operiod of calm, extending over several weeks. litstin, who fully believed that the deeds of the estate were in existence- somewhere, searched high and low for the missing documents, and hoped almost against hope that before Quarter-day came he would be ablaie to flourish them in the face of Lozal Tregeagle's &lowan&

lltu the numerous closets and cupboards and presses of the old house, letters and %papers had accumulated for a hundred and fifty-years, and to go through each bundle carefully no only required time but an infinite amount of patience. During the first week Justin did little or- nothing else. Then came an offer from Captain Tom Bassett„ who, with his two brothers, Richard and Manuel, owned Treskiddy Mine on the other side of the. valley. This offer was too good to .be lightly thrown, aside. The Bassett brothers were working miners,. They knew all about "lodes," and "drifts," and "cross-cuts," and "faults." They knew also how- to extract the tin from the ore, and were authori-. ties on "strips," and "wracks," and "buddlbs." But the corajnenial side of the business they knew, practically nothing about. Book-keeping was, a science they had never mastered, and the usages of the commercial world occasioned them consilerable umasiness.

They had started several years previously fo,work Treskiddy as a private venture, and being- frugal and industrious men and the price of tin also taking a turn for the better, they managed' to make a little money. This they spent in further develop- ing their property till, by-and-bye, tley bectuno men of oome importance. in the parish of St. Tag°. But. the old habits of doing cvelything them- selves clung to 0:on ; while the idea of having a stranger to keep their accounts was most repugnant to thorn. So Manuel superintended affairs under- ground, Richard was"Cap'n " on tNe "floors," and Tom, being the eldest, did the buying and selling, and was, in fact, general manager. Of late, however, Captain Tore had felt that he was getting entirely out of his depth. The business of the mine had increased very considerably ; the number of men, women, and boys employed was larger than ever before; and the wage-sheet had grown to vcry considerable dimensions. Captain Tom did his best to keep his books in proper order; but, in spite of all his efforts, backed up as they were by the assistance of his brothers, his accounts got beyond him. So perplexed was he at times that he did not know on which side the balance was, or indeed if there was any balance at all. Moreover, in making contracts for timber, and tools, and machinery, and powder and fuse, and the general stores of a mine, he felt that he was at a disadvantage. His excursions into arithmetic had never advanced beyond a simple rule of three sum. Hence, when prices ran off into &chili's, and sellers talked about point this and that, and gave him quotations in the unfamiliar jargon of the Stock Exchange and enlarged on the subject of discounts and the Bank-rate, and other matters that Captain Tom knew nothing about, he felt, in a vague way, that he was at their mercy, and that they wuld cheat him right and left, without his knowing anything about it. .

, Evenitrafter evening the brothers sat with their 1 heads together, trying to straighten things out. ' .Prosfierity had its drawbacks as well as its advan- tages. They, had become, people of considerable thaportanceln' the parish, and as large employers of labottl•-i—that is, large Piz St. lago—were looked up to and crmsulted in all local affairs; but the responsibilities more than outweighed the honours. They were really happier in the old days than now. Justin arrived home when Captain. Tom's per- , plexity had reached an acute stage. For several evenings the btothera•had discussed the advisability of bringing innn Outsider to assist in the manage- ment of the commercial -side of their .business. But who couldi they get? It was no joke letting a stranger inicKtlieir secret/. He might land them in worse diffithrltiee than those from which they were now trying to escape. "How would' young Pentyre do ? " suggested Manuel, slowlyiarid diffidently, as they sat together one evening in earnest confabulation. The others looked up with a questioning expres- sion in their eyes; but did not venture any reply. "He's honesk.at any rate," went on Manuel, feeling as though lie had been thrown upon the defensive, "and we've known him ever since he Was a boy." , "Aye, that's tree-enough, "assented Richard. "And he's had' ir good deal a experience," con- tinued Manuel. "He pmetirAlly managed them stores doyrn at Trelford, and since then he's been to London, and inn al very .important situation too, they do say." Richard and Tom looked at their brother with great interest, and waited for him to enlarge upon the theme; but Manuel had exhausted all his stodk of arguments, and was perforce reduced to silence. Captain Tom sighed at length, and remarked that they might do worsev. Manuel's face brightened. "What do you think of it, Richard?" he questioned. "I wee with Tom, 'was the reply. The ice was now fairly broken,, and for the next hour Justin's merits and demerits were discussed with Much animations:. . On the following morning Captain Tom came across to Endilloe, and with much diffidence and circumlocution, - broached the matter to Justin, explaining, it the same time, with considerable candour, the reasons for the innovation. Had Justin been offered the post of Home Secretary he could' scarcely, Have been more surprised. , It will require time, to. think about," he said. "If you will give metro fewdaye; I will let you know."

, Captain Tom wasinanifestly disappointed. The possibility of Justin declining: the offer had never once occurred to eithin-rof.the brothers. "If you think the salary is too small." he said, with energy, "I'll spring another five pound ; there now." "It is not a question, of salary at all," Justin answered, with a smiles "It must know first what I am undertaking." '"But you know all 'bent buying and selling?" persisted Captain Tom. "I understand some markets frirly well," Justin said, evasively. "And you be gootintefigures?'"' "Fairly good." "And you know sehnt•book-keeping is?" "Yes." "Then you are inst•the man. for the job. Say yes and have done with it." "Let me walk acrass•with you,to the mine and. • go mole fully into. the matter; Tustin persisted. It would be fooliile-fer me to undertake what I cannot possibly perferm." "Oh, you can de it right, enough," Captain Min said, impatiently. "It"s as easy as winkin' to a man as understands figures." Nevertheless Jdatin spent two whole days at Treskiddy, and A/Ibn, announced that he would undertake the position and'dceltis best. Dorothy was delighted„ while- John regarded it .as a direct interposition. of' Providence.. For the next two or three weeks tlis search for lost docu- ments at home was left entirely in the hands of Dorothy, but without.suceess.. Dorothy's hope had lain in a strong oaken chest; built into the wall and so forming a:, windowsseato at the top of the stairs. This chest thad'eridently been intended,as a receptacle for valuable•dtxtuments. Its corners were clamped with brass, while'dte lock- was strong enough for a churels door:. Dorothy spent hours kneelirg-before this, ant, for it was full tchthe brim of papers of ali sorts. Some of the documents. were so interesting that she forgot arlq about..the object of her search. Letters writtervbphaiadtv.lonFsince mouldered into dust carried her-beak- in imagination to a time -When the Peaky:es were. people of considerable importance in tlibicouaty.. On the' leftlhand side, was a set of drawers occupying the entire width of the box from top to bottom. Sores of' these &ewers were folk of love- letters careftany.tieel:witkribbon. Dorothy .read: a.f6w, of them; she, eetvld not help it. Rojas,. sill the people were dead and forgotten, BO what' did' it matter? 131.0 some of those old love-letters stied her heart very strangely. They mighb have been written only yeqerday. The wonitl' had doubtless changed a good deal in a, hundred•years, but the human heart remained th same._ owreasy it weard be to con- struct a romance•out or those old 'letters. Those early Pentyres loved;. andl hoped, and. despaired, as she had done.. Andl theta she fell tw thinking of Tom Pendavris,, and' the letters faded front her ;Bight and" tionespassedl away unheeded. What an -age it seemed' situ° he went away, and no single word hachtemen brea the long siiience. Had he forgotten-her:Po gad' lle failed in the struggle of life?, Was lose wasted? Would he never come back tolies again ? She &ow, a Fong sigh after awlite, and said to herself that A. didn't matter. That in a few years sherwoarld' haws gone the way of the other Pentyres ; that in, the grave there. was neither love nor regret ; .tet in the coining years her love-story would he ttgi more, tw anyone than the love stories containedin those &did letters.

nt:ght be quite. true. But such philosophising brenght her no.satisfaction. Tom Pinds.rvis was eiserything to her now, and the tssurance..c..t his I.twe was of tnose importance than ereerything else• ea earth. . _

- - But in, spite at day dreams the search went steadil3- mu. Vilma Justin had got the affairs of the,Bassonb brottors into something like shape, he was able to join Dorothy signin in the quest. But nothinviame of it, and Quatter-day was drawing pprilous#. near. Bice, meanwhile, was keeping quiet and playing al waiting- game, He did net know how much was behind! Jiistin's game of bluff; and was sometimes inclined to think that their position was much naive secure than he had imagined. He was afraid to play. a bold game lest in the end all his cards should be trumped; that was the one contingency.... he dreaded. If the Pentyres got the upper handl of him he would be the, laughing stock of thn wholb district. Ile knew that nobody loved hinkt, and that there wasn't a man in the parish of St.. lage. Who wouldn't rejoice to see him worsted game of As Quarter-day drew,' near Justin grew desperstuf and at length, from a strategic point of view, did, an exceettmgly foolish thing. Instead of goir.g to the mine one morning he walked to Trelford, and was soon closeted witt Lawyer Nankivel. The old lawyer listened to Justin's storyorith quiet interest, and when it warended said, irr,quite a matter-of-fact soot of way: "Are you quite certain that the deeds yus,have been searching for ever existed?" Justin started and then his face fell. "At," he said, lowly, !‘1 have no absolute prooft As .a. matter of fact we halt always taken it for ranted." "You ghoul& take nothing for granted, the old' Lawyer said, sententiously. "But in such a ease we had a right boy" Justin, answered, with spirit. "Endilloe has been in the. possession et the rentyres . for generatktus. Thera, must have been a title to the property originally." "That kr no %peen follows. People got property, in curious ways in olden times. Tre.geagle hitnseff" would have a &faculty in showing title for. half of his possessions." "But ho mannges to 1 eep them."' _ . . _
" Exact ly. better claim."
-None disputes hist right or shame&

--rtan-drii;ei a foul shame that he. should dispute or right," Justin said, bitterly: "Because he is lord and rich he can play thit tyrant or the rogue with impunity." Tho lawyer smiled but did not reply. lestin bit kis lip, and for a few moments was silent, then he sai3: ?re you sure that you have not the deeds in an Jot your numerous safes and boxes P " 'Quite sure." "Have you ever looked for them t "No, I have not. There has been no necessity.l! "Will you make a search ? This is a matter of considerable importance to us." "If you particularly wish it, yes. But you can hardly expect me to waste my time and the time of my clerks for nothing." "I expect nothing of the kind," Justin said, sharply. 'I expect your accounts have always been settled when thev have been sent in.°

"Cif course they have I did not mean UV roggest anything of the kind:" Justin went back to his work feeling anything but ' hopeful, but he tur'S4pated no immediate ' trtnable.' HOW Mr. Bice got' to know what transpired in the lawyer's office is not for anyone to say. Suffice it he did get to know, and he rubbed his hands with great-glee. "Now.l'm absolutely certain," he said to himself. "The youngfool has played into my hand's beautifully." Mr. Nankivel concluded histearch on June 19th, and sent word at .a.ce that the deeds were not in his possession On June 20th' Mr. Bice sent in his ultimatum. It was short and to the point. If they were not out of the house' by the 25th they were to talie the consequences of the law. More- ozer, if they offered any resistance summary measures would be adopted. Also claim would be made for arrears of rent in respoet of all the years that John Pontyre had occupied If.ndilloe. (To be continued.)

Ityi portant Business. The Municipal Bowliag Green Question.

A meeting of the Warrington Town Council was held RU the COULICiI Chamber at the Town Hall, Warriugton, on Tuesday evening. Tne Mayor (Alderman Roberts) Presided, and there were also present :—Aldermen Fair. dough, Heaton, Shaw Green, Hutchinson, Monks, Frit:r- -oom:a, Councillors A J Jolley, Plumpton, Wilkinson, James EVilal, Tinnion, John Evans, Bennett, 8 Davies, Baird, John Roberts, Burton, Peacock, F R Roberts, William Roberts, Brough, A Jolley, Sampson, Duncan, Ellison, Rogers, L Greening, Malkin, Hulse, with J L Whittle (towu clerk), S Wilson (depute town .clerk), J Fairhurst (borough treasurer), T Longdin (borough surveyor), W H Grirnsdale (electrical engineer), W Haddock (gas engineer). J Sutcliffe (deputy /borough Surveyor), Dr J Guest Gornall (deputy medical officer of health). The Election of Auditors. The MAYOR announced that Messrs Bradshaw and Harrison had ueen elected elective auditors and that he had appointed Councillor A J Jaley as his auditor for the easuiog year. Watch Committee. Technical Instruction. At a meeting of the above committee it was resoLved that the tender of Messrs James Smith and Company (D,rhy), L'inited, to supply police clothing be accepted, aud that of Nie:srs II naworth Bros to supply prl:i,ze caps, helmets, Ate A conference having been held to co :shier arrangements to be made for the Technical Instruction Classed, now held in the Old Armoury, which is required to be taken down for tire erection of the new parade- room, it was resolved : Teat in the opinion of the con- ference temporary arrangements should be made for the accommodation of married constables and that the Old fiemaury should be allowed to stand for the present." The Borough Surveyor was ins:meted to report as to the Cost of the proposed alterations. the MAYOR proposed the adoption of the minutes. Althrmaa HEATON seconded, and the motion was tarried. The following recommendations made by the members of the Lighting Sub-Committee and a deputetem from the Gas Committee, were approved : (1) That the Gas Committee be requested when hying mains in new streets to make provision for fixing street lamps. (2) That for the guidance of the Gas Committee and for improving the lighting of the streets, due regard being had to the 'Wilting of the aide streets and back Passages, lamps shall not be erected in main streets at a Pester distance than 40 yards apart,in secondary streets riot more than 50 yards apeman:l in the tilde streets and back passages not more than 60 yards apart. (4) That all orders for fixing lamps be Riven by tile Lighting Sub Committee: The minutes were confirmei, on the motion of Coun- Ciller BENNETT, seconded by Councillor Penneeroe. The Sanatorium at Sankey. Alterations in the Original Scheme. 1 „ At a meeting of the Health Committee it was resolved rat the amended plans now submitted by the Borough ?orveyor for the sabatorium at Sankey be approved,sub-1 es:t te the main pavilion being reduced to a 12-bed ward. I lii coesequence of the Local Government Board having "N▪ niree the erection of an additional ward, to hold four be, as an observation ward. a.he Mayoa moved the adoption of the minutes. Alderman HuTCeINSON seconded. . Councillor BURTON referred in terms of disparagement 'tithe alterations in the original generale for tae erection Ze the small pox hospital or sanatorium at Sankey, 'hese they had hal to reduce the accemmedation ?I:o 24 beds te 12 beds, It se -med to him rather a big ree'ah down, and the accommodation very small for the e,;')4et of money to be expended. div.head: Recreation of the Ratepayers
div.p: The Recreation of the Ratepayers
to the Fore.

The Town Hall Park awl Baths Committee at a meet- ing heti on February 21st, considered t- bu:ated return of ifif ortnation obtained from other towns with reip-oct to the cast of constricting and maintaining public bow- log greens. After full consideration, and in view of the difficulty of obtaining suitable sites, it was resolved that the question of providing public biwling greens be deferred for one year. Alderman Heirost moved the confirmation of the minutes. _

Alderman literceitesoer seconded. • Councillor BENNETT referred to the resolution deferr- ing the provision of public bowling-greens for a year. Lie remarked that he did see that the Council would be in a different position a year hence. They had a perk in the middle of the town, as well ao Queen's Gardens, and Victoria Park, and in one or the other a bowling grog . might be provided. A request for accommodation of that kind on behalf of a certain section of the people of the tewn was a very proper one, and he was person- ally disappointed that tee committee was not able to proceed with the matter at once. Councillor Teams EveteS expressed a similar opinion, and contended Viet the laud oehind Bank H min was a very suitable site for a howling green. Last summ or it was fit to play lawn tennis on, and he saw the tackle. : (Laughter.) He nougat that if the land could be used for lawn tennis it could be used for bowling. He centen- ded that the ratepayers were entitled to have a b wling greee. It had been said teat there were ample bowling greens in the town.No doubt there were but they were in connection with political club 3, and there wore nuineers of persona who did net care to go to a political clue but who would be delighted to have a game of bowls else. wnere. Bowling was a healthy recreation, and if his suggestion was acted upon the site would be very suit- able as it Was walled off trom the rest of the park, as hoped the committee wend at once proceed to make a bowling green there, as there Was a very general feeling that the Corporation should provide some kind of recrea- tion for the working men in the public perke. (dear, hear.) Councillor MALKIN said there were many people who did not care to come within the" taint" of a political club, and he °lntended that tin committee were respell_ sible for the " moral, social, and enjoyable recreation " of the people. Ho hoped the provision of a bowling green would be again taken into consideration. He was surprised one had not already b en provided. Councillor TrieteioN observed chat the resolutioe of the committee was a very clever method of shelving the vestion. At the same time he admitted that that might not be their intentioa,bet it would have that result, lie moved as an amendment that the resolution referring to the howling greens be referred back to the committee for further consideration. The resolution of the committee did not finally settle the question:: it did not say whether the cemmittee would or would not provide a green. There were three greens in connection - with the political clubs of the town and others in connection with the hotels, but the people who used those greens were not the class of peoole he would cater for. It was the work- line classes he would cater for, who thought they should haves ime part of the rate 3 of the borough spent in their particular interest. Be contended that the money spent in the provision of a bowling-green would be well spent, and that the Corporation would get something back towards its cost. A green would net altogether be a pecuniary loss to the town. Councillor A J JOLLEY seconded the amendment. Alderman llorcalesoe sp•ike against the amendment and suggested that the matter should be brought forward again next October. Councillor PEACOCK supported the amend Gent and remarked that it was .00t lung since th at they passed a large sum for the erection of Turkish baths. Councillor GREENING sail he thought a bowling green was a proper thiug to have, He subinit:ed a resolution at the committ:ie that they should move in the matter, but he could not get a seconder. It would cost £250 for a green and £l5O a year to keep it going, but he did net mind even teat sum as it would be money well spent. It was nct fair to say that the committee were going about ma roundabout Way to shelve the matter. Councillor TINNION : It looks like it.

Councillor GUI33;;N•G Tue ..e-o-as-Mittee honestly Shelved the question for a short period only or I should have brought the matter forward. I moved :ao amend- ment but could get no seconder. Ce=Miler PLOSIpTON contended that the committee was a standing-atalt sort of committee. Taey did not appear to move at all. (Laughter). The work in coo- -1 nectioa with the Turkish baths and the roundiag .off of I the wall in Froghall-lane, and other qaestions which bad been passed by the Council liad not ben carried out. Alderman HEAT3N : There is nothing on the minute,' about the Turkish baths. I hope Councillor Plumpton will keep to the minutes. (Laughter), Councitlor PLIMPTON : We want a little bit of fire on the part of the committ e. (Renewed Laughter). The MAYO 3 : You are wrong in attributing the neglect in toe rounding off of the corner of the street to , the rown Hall Committee. I believe that is the work of the Street Improvement Committee. Councillor nustgroti : If ao, I .11.urit apologize, because I know the Street COoitnittee.are anxious to do the work. • Councillor Jowl Hussars observed that there was no intention on the part oi the committee to shelve the question of the greens. The Meroa said he was strongly in favour of the pro- vision of municipal howling greens, and he was glad the matter was raking hold of the public mind. Whatever was expended in providing for the recreation and health of the oureesser was money well spent and was ulii- mately economical a, well. The question of expense did not appeal to him one bit. In tne same way that they had provided for Curkiah Bates so they must—and every progressive municip4ity must—provide additi-enal means of recreation tor the people at large. (Rear, hear.) There was a large constituency which objected to being associated directly with th 3 very obj clionable Liberal Club.—(laeghter)—and he was going to say the Still more cijectionahle Conservative Club (Renewed laughter). After they had taken the bowling greens nut of those institutions they had none except what were connected with puhlichonQes,

Critineilier JOHN ROBSRTS : Arp'ey. The Mayon : 'l'ha is confined principally to the wealthy aristocracy of Warrington. (Ltegliter): It i 9 in no sense iatentlel for working an who pay the biggest p •irtion of the rates .nd are, therefore, entitle's to some coniideration• (Hear, bear.) His lfforsi)p sweeared that instead of going to a vote the resolution of the Committee eimu'd h wichdrasto, the Committee to pronent a teport to the Camell at the aest anelag or
wo months hence. It was impassible to provide a green this seas in.

Alderman HEATON said it was ir.itendr,d to include the nest of tn.- p:ovision f a bJwliag green in'tbe estimates for this sear. He did not want to have a green in a backyard. be c iet of a green would be £5OO or £6OO. However, be would withdraw the resolution. He would ee',; into a row, but he had o doubt he would come out of it as well aN any member of the CJUUCIi could. (Laughtec.) Tlvne would be a storm in a tea-pt, bat he had no doubt it would soon blow over. He wouid promise th it the questidia would be again censidered by the Coinmittee, (dear, bear). Councillor Triisros said it would do no harm to go to the vote. It would help the committee. Alderman HEAToN : We do not want any help. _ .
COUROill,r TINNION :Th =lre ore L tj2c LJ Watidraw tbc amendment. Alderman tittaTox : Th 3 c)xunitteo will report upon the matter as suggested._
Councilor 11 N-NTON : Oa that definite promise I will withlre.w the anr-ndment.
Ti2o minutes were hen comirmeci with the exception of the on dpferriag tie b3wling green q restion, which was withdrawn.

At a meeting of the Wit r Committee on February the To Na Cl,,.rk submitted a revlrt of Mr William Dwell on the negotiations for the purchase of land at Appleton. A report by the Deptry-Chairmen and the Water Engineer on the plans uquired for D pumping Station was real, and it was resolved that on their recommendation the following type of engine, viz., deep-well, triple expansion inverted vertical surfac.; condensing bell-crank beam engine, having a modern arrangement of stearn receiver, cylinders steam jacketed, and an up-to-dato arrangemenr. of Corliss valve gear, with asp ,rate well and high lift pumps, be adopted, and that et the request of the Chairman of the Tech.ical Instruction Committee, Mr Fletcher, the c'erk of the works at the high level reservoir, be allowed to act as clerk.of works of the New Technical Schools.

At a meeting of the Electric Lighting Committee, Mr Preec3 having certified that in his judgment it aas proper for the Corporation to take possession and com- plete the work undertakea by the Clayton Eogmeering- Company, Ltd., under clause 39 of the contract with that company, it was resolved that the Town Clark give notice to the company that ths Corporation had t .ken ptoss.ssion of the p act and would complete the work. Mr Preece also reported that, in his opiaion, in vi.w of the probable early introduction of electrical tram ways, It was desirable that additions should be made to the plant at the works, and it was resolved that the engineers be requested to prepare estimates of the cost of such additional plant, and that Mr Grimatiale be in- etrucced to prepare an estimate of the coat of the pro- bable extension of mains.

Alderman MONKS, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said the members of tho Council would know that there had been a considerable amount of delay in having the station started,and that had been due almost entirely to what he might call the carelersness on the part of an engineering company and the little desire they had shown to puth the work forward. It was rather a strong step they had taken, but hl felt and the com- mittee felt they were perfectly justified, and that it was necessary to take it if the work war Co be completed satisfactorily. Members of the Council would have noticmi that a certain ammnt of progress had been made 'during the last month. They had now got No 2 engine working satisfactorily and since it had been going the street lamps had been put on altovther, with a part also of the markets, and as fir as he had heard the general opinion was that the lighting was satisfactory although it might be improved It would he improve!, because the mains had been lying unused for so long that they had got rather out of condition. As they were used they would came into tv.ter working order and the arc lamps would give a more brilliant light than at the present time. With regard to tha last paragraph in the report he sxolained that the work was now equal to the amount which Mr Preece estimated in his original rep )rt in Decembrr, 1893. In that report Mr Preece estimated that the Cor- poration wou'd have an incoins from the sa o of 150.900 unite per annum which was equal to eight thousand eight-candle power lamps. On Saturday night. the light- ing load at the electric station Was about equal to that. They were now using for lighting purposes and for driving several small motors p raver eqaal to about ten thousand eig4t-candle-power lamps. They would see that as far as the sale was concerned they were making satisfactory progress, and there was every reason to believe that by next winter the extension of the plant would bej 'stifled. That was why the engineers had been requested to prepare estimates and wheo they were , ready it was proposed in submittiag them to toe Council to go further into detail. , The DEPUTY MAYOn seconded.

CounMlor GREENING elsid he was gad t hear such a good account of the work. Be appcoved of the action of the committee in regard to the queEtion of the non- fulfilment of tha contract, and aiked whether any loss vac cover.d by a penalty clause in the agreemPnt. Alderman MONKS: The Oast will be deducted from the contract, and the c inunittee will not 1: put to any additional expense. rho minutes were then approved. Proposed Tramway s. Discussion on the Overhead Trolley System.

N 1 isms Preece and Cardew having reported to the Tramways Committee on the cost of tne construction of the tramway from Sankey Bridg,is to Kuistaford-road, Swing Bridge, and having submitted specifications for the work, it was resolved that they be instructed t ) obtain tenders for the constructiou and equipment of the tramway. At a further meeting it was resolved that ths General purnorps Committee be requested to present a petition to Parliammt against the Soutn L4ncashire Tramways Bill. rtie cammittess again 'considered the draft agresoneat suninitted by the proms;ori of the Warriogton and Northwich Light Railway., and it was resolved that Msjor Cardew be requeved t) attend the next meeting of this Committee to advise mem On ' the engineering provisions of the prop seed agreement. A letter was read from the Board of Trade giving their consent to a croising ol the level of tramway No 10 over the London and North Western Railway Company's Warrington and Steckport Line, subject to compliance with the provisions of S-iction 10 of too Order, cud the approval of that department to toe safety arrangements at the croising. Trio Ni• Yon proposed the adoption of the minutes. He said the only resolution that required any explana- tion was in regard to the presanta,ion of a petition to Parliament against tha South Lancashire Tramways Sill. Ibis 4r3:109 was ,Akeri merely for the purp.sse of obtain. ing a locus standi la order to protect any intresis which might come under d scussion during the cerisida•ation of the bill before the House of Commons Committee. Alderman &Tonics ssconded.

In doing so, he sal tqa Council had IDA the matter be- fore them on several occasions but he did not think the Council had ever hstl any definite statem .nt present sr to the various kinds of elew:ric tractioa and the neces- sity of adoptinsr, the overhead system before all others. Ile had always argued that;the overhead system was ex- tretnely Unsightly but perhaps that was not ma argu- ment which wei4had very strongly with some memt era. The town was supposed to 133 80 ugly that a little wore ugiiness was quite immaterial. (Laughter.) a large extent was being done in Warringten, but after all there would be a certain amo ant of danger in con- nection with the overhead system. Some authorities had decided against it, and one or the most Important— tee London Comity Council—if er the fulleet cressime centideration had :ejected the overhead system. That in itself was a strong argumeat for con- sideration. He had also read an article in the" Man- chester Guardian," begging the Manchester Cceperatioa to hesitate before it committed itself to the scheme which existed at Liverpool. There were, of ()mese, ar- guments in favour of it, but he did no; wish the Cor- poration to commit themselves to it without the fullest possible information. Mr Bennett proaealed to refer to the four ithernative sYstems, but stated that be did not profess to underlstand them. lie did not think the mat- ter was one of great urgency. It Could stand over for a little while and in the meantime the information asked for could be obtained. Councillor TINNION said he ferment' seconded the amendment in order to get further information. He was talking to an exp2rienced gentleman on the subject who told him that it would be more a Ivantageous in the long run if the electric tube arrangement could be adapted. Alderman SEM,' Garotte was of opini iu that the matter had been allowed to drift. He did root think any mem- ber of tree Council had been furnished with any inform- ation as to the probable c let of the tram way as agreed to be carried out or any figures given as to Oa estimated income which might be expected Co be derived from it. He did not think that toe traffics would result in a profit and he would like to have , some information as to the basis on welch the committee bad acted in going se far as to ask for tenders. lie thought it was u edersteod that some information was to be given t the Council, and he would like to have it before taking such a step as that now proposed. Councillor at R ROBKRTS said he could.uot help think- ing that it was the preoer thing to support the amend- ment. Steins: that there was considerable searceine of heart in many towns with regard to the ovetbeaii system, the Council ought Co have full and adsqu ate in- formation before they accepted the reseluceou. Tney ought to have some information as to how such a fright- ful catastrophe a. that at Liverpool cued be avoided. He should also like to know why tbe telephone Coda- party had desired it to be publicly known that it W3S their intention Co put all their wires underground. The Corporation ought not to adopt a system like the one proposed, which was fraught with' such danger, until they knew what they were doing. As intelligent men ' they ought to kraow what they were cominitting them- selves to. He had every admiration for the desire of the committee to proceed with th o construction of tramways. The ante-deluvian 'bus service in Warrington was a joke to all visitors to the town and the sooner it was abolished the better for all concerned, but in avoiding one danger do not let them run into another. They would be con• tent to ride on wet 'buses for another yea: or two if by so doing they were able to avoid a frightfu. catastrophe, such as occtsrred in Liverpool. taderman MONKS remarked that it was rather late in the day for members of the Council to raise objections. The report of Messrs. Preeee and Cardew, who were the Council's advisers in the matter, was laid before the Council twelve months ago, and the report specifically stated that the trim ways would be fully cq sipped with the overhead trolley system. No intention was then raised, an 1 having adopted the system the Council c mid not very well entertain some other system now. He did notseimit that tee overhead system was un- sightly; it was a matter of arrangcntentaiuct it could be so arranged as not to hi unsightly. With regard to danger, there might be Some little danger, but steps were boing taken to miaineise it. The telephone com- pany bad teetered into an agreement with the Corpora• don under which they proposed t lay all their wires underground. Annual Meeting. r. C El Woo prsi led over the &urinal meeting of the Warrington Swimming Club which was held in the Corporation Ba:ts, Legn-street, on Monday evening. Amongst others presenr were : Messrs T Locker F Oar- side, R T Harding, C Houghton, J Boscow, W Sutton, J Bate, with A G Robertson and J Gray (joint hon. seem- tams).
THE ANNUAL REPORT.

Mr. GRAY read the Sscretary'a report which stated I titt it could hardly be said that the work of the 1900 season had been a success. The amount received from members' subieriptioas was £l6 14s 61, against £l6 133 6 1 111 1899, thus showing an increase Of Is, but there had been hose on tto year's working of £3 44 4d. This was due Lo-the gala, held on October 514 Many things conspirel against the sueeetS of the event, but the greatest was the General Election, The gala posters were lost among the electioneering notices, and the gala followed the night of the poll In this town. It should tic rem,mbered that the date of the gala was fixed be- ; fore the date of the poliiag for the election was known. I A loss of £1.3 7. 51 resulted. Again, in the polo matches I the club did badly. They bid greatly missal the Brothers Ashton, and it Wa.s hoped that there might be some likelihood of thoir returning from the front shortly. or the fortheaining SEASOR the club had secured the North v. Midlands Polo match, whioh of course would be played at the Warrington Baths, and at which tney would have all the "crack" men in the Nore.h and Midlands. A hearty vote of thanks was due to Mr T,LockerAnd Mr S B samont, who on one °cession when the polo team was short, went in and played themselves. At the gala Mr Locker acted as hon. starter. The balance sheet showed that after 174% Inc, all ex- penses, there was a balance in hand of £ll 141 83' The report and balance sheet were adopLed. THE PRESIDENT.

div.p: ELECTION OF BOROUGH AUDITORS.
Result of the Poll.

On Feiday the ratepasers of Warrington had the eloper tunity of elacting two auditors fJr the Borough. By a curioua anomaly although two auditors had to be elected each ratepayer could only vote for one candidate, Of the four candidates who entered the field, Mr John Harrison was the only one who had proviously heti the office of borough auditor. His late colleague, Mr James 11-iton,did n stalk reaelectioo"as a protest against the manner in w 114313 the auditors have been recently treated.'

Mr John Harrisin of 4, Egyr-street, was the adopted candidate of the Liberal party,and Mr A H Erosfield,the chaittnan of the Association issued a circular, in which he stated that Mr Harrison "ii thoroughly conversant with the duties of the office, having held the position for 17 years, and during that period he has glven entire satisfaction to the ratepayers at large." . .
Mr Elwin Beadshavr, chartered accountant, of Egypt stre(t, had the fillppOrt ot the Conaerva'Avo Association..

Mr. Martin nonagon, of 151, 04 ford-lane, iron worker, was supported by the Warrington Trades and Labour Council: In the course of his address to tho eleetors, Mr Fianagan says :—The contracts scan- dal. of which you have heard so much, and which is tjll a.itating the public mind, is by no means at an end: It is therefore necessary that you should be rep• resented by au:A i whose actions will be free from tho influences of political partizanship, and who are not in any way interested in, or likely to take into considera- tion, " as a matter of business," ne limited companies in which so many of our aldermen and couricilldris arfl directors and shareholders, . . . lam not employea by, nor have I any intereat in, fi:ras trading with thes Corporation, therefore no inducement to screen thoSe, who have.

Mr. Samuel Gough, of Winwick•street,house furnisher was the nominee of the Ratepayers and Property Owners • Asiocistion. In his addrPas Mr. Gough q iotes Deem— ster Shee and the late Lord Chief Justice on the duties of auditors., and tra,k9s a Dumber of 553ert1005 relating to memtere of the CorporatiJn, the accuracy of whicb is questionable.

The polling booth was at the Gymnasium, Palmyra- ' ecoare, where there were three polling stations, namely, one for tbe Town Hall, Whitecross and Bewsey Wards., one for the Orford, St, John's and Fairfield wards, and one for the Howley, Bt, Austin's and Latchford Wards. At polling-station No 1, Mr C H llsworch acted as presiding officer, and Mr Joseph Smith as poll clerk, while at polling station N 3 2, the presiding offices was Mr W 11 J Jenkins, and the poll clerk Mr George X Vernon. At No 3 polling station the above posilone were respectively held by Mr Thomas Cooper. and Mr I Alfred Clive. Polling commenced at eight o'clock and continued until eight in the (veiling. The ballot papers were View conveyed to the Town Hall, where the work of connting was proceeded with.

div.head: TLiE COUNIING OF THE VOTES.
div.p: TLiE COUNIING OF THE VOTES.

All the candidates were preset in the Council Chamber at the counting of the votes. It was ascer. mined that 1.440 electors had voted. There were no fewer than 28 spoiled papers, 27 of them containing votes for more than one candidate, and one unmarked. It may be bete stated for the pur- pose of comnariou that at the last elecim of Borough auditors 1487 tlectors recorded their votes rgainst 1440 on Friday. It wia therefore b 3 seen that there were 47 fewer votes recorded.

At the conclusion of the counting it was found that Mr Edwin Bradshaw heath(' the poll with 502 votes, idr John Harrison being second with 448 Mr Martin Flanagan polled 288 votes and Mr Saul Gough 174. Mr BRADSHAW proposed a vote of [hanks to the Mayor and the Town Clerk and officials for the imptrtial manner in which they had conducted the el, ctiou. He said that neither Mr Harrison nor himmeli had intro- duc,xl personalities into the election, and he hoped that Mr. Flanagan and Mr. Gough would take the defeat with good grace.

Mr. filealtisox said had much pleasure iu seconding the vote of thanks. Mr FLLNAGAN supp.)rled t,ho vote of thanks. Although beaten, he said, be had eu,u4h grit lett in him to fight again and in Whatova position he was elccted be would 00 his duty. Mr Goucar did not speak, and the vote was nnani- mously carried.

The Mayon acknowledged the compliment, arid stated that so far as his duties as returning (Act- were con- cerned, they, wero not very onerr.u.. The Town Clerk had carried our, tip?. dutica with biS u6ual ability and to the satisfaction of all concerned.

Every Liberal must desire Parliamentary Decency. to preserve the decency of Parliament as well as the liberty of protest and debate. A scene like the one at mianight on Tuesday is indefensible. Members of Parliament, ft om whatever quarter of the United Kingdom they may come, must comply with the rules of Parliamentary life. Sallie of these rules may be rather irksome to the passionate and troublesome to the proud. They may check the unruly and avert the disorders which sometimes may appear to be the only way of making a protest sensational. But they apply to all, they are fair, and no assembly can exist without rules and with- out making provision for their enforcement. AS the Speaker ruled, it is not a question of privilege but of order. The Irish members have had a good many opportunities this session of taking part in public bosiness, and they have made abundant use of them. Their action on Tuesday night was in the highest degree irregular and disorderly. At the same time we must not shut our eyes to the what we may fairly describe as the unprece- dented conduct of the Government in relation to the House of Commons. It is hardly decent to give private members a chance of balloting for bills and motions and then to swoop down and take away half their time, under the excuse that Government has so much business that it cannot attend to it without suspending the ordinary standing orders and regulations. Parlia- ment ought to have met earlier, it ought to have had an ordinary autumn session, and there ought not to have been supplementary estimates for millions sterling to interfere with the orderly pro- gress of business. The Government alone is re- sponsible for the muddle which has interfered with the ordinary course of events and has exasperated opponents. As Mr. Bannsv,a conservative mem,- ber,declares, " we are becoming a despotic nation," The act which provoked the scene of Tuesday was an act of despotism. A supplementary estimate for £17,304,000 had been asked for, and only one subject had been fully debated, whereupon Mr- BALFOUR proceeded to closure the main question, in order to obtain the vote on account at a single sitting. Surely there was no absolute necessity tO take this extraordinary course? The discussion might have been continued on Thursday without any injury to a single department or Parliamen- tary procedure. But it is not Mr. BaLroules way. He was in the Lords all the time the discussion was proceeding there, and he allowed his colleagues to attend to business in the Commons, thinking, no doubt, that lie could closure the debate whenever he pleased. He too fond of this exercise of arbitrary power, and it is to be feared he does not always think of the decency of debate and Ministerial self-control and conciliation. The closure cannot be systems' tically used without its becoming an abuse and an engine of despotism. The House of Common finds its liberties curtailed at almost every point. The private members have got their Wednesdaye t Easter, and after that the House of Commons will become a Chamber to register the wishes and decrees of the Government. We do not hesitate to say that this view of the House of Commons le a violation of the Constitution. The country% wishes are not all made known by an indolent majority, led bya weak Government and a closure using Leader of the House. If it were so the op' ponents of the Government might just as well be denied admission to the House of Commons, all debate being regardeu as an indecency and a sir perfluity.We seem to be g.itting well on the waY to such a state of things. and Tuesday's scene mei open our eyes to a real peril.

Whatever else happens Controlling the we must hold fast to the British Army. doctrine of Parliaments*? control of the army, arid that can only be in deo' ger when we go to sleep and allow the militad element to become supreme. But we shall hale to modify the practice by concessions to the weel‘' ness of human nature. attempt, and a nice mess he has made of it. The Commander-in-Chief did not do enough, accord- ing to Government theory. He should have been More insistent, pushful, determined and enter- Prising. Why he did not so act we can readily guess ; he was always confronted With a masterful Socretary of War, who had behind him the Committee of National Defence and the Cabinet. LORD LANSDOWNE has not been retained in his position so that. Vie must assume that even his colleagues, and at any rate the PRIME MINISTER, were not satisfied

With his exploits. He began the war preparations U apparent ignorance of the real strength of the Boers, and the result has long been apparent to us all. We have now got a new Secretary for War, a Weaker civilian than Lord LANSDOWNE, but we have in Earl ROBERTS probably a more powerful and experienced Commander-in-Chief than Lord WOLSELEY. is the control of the army to undergo nO change whatever, more than is implied in the: -selection of two new officials likely to get on better together than Lord LANSDOWNE and Lord WOLSELEY did? If so, we are certain to suffer, and our military system will combine extravag- ance in expenditure with weakness and inefficiency. The country wants to have a good army, under Parliamentary control, and it does not want per- sonal wrangles and Parliamentary attacks. There raust be a better separation of the functions Of the two officials, and it is possible to arrange it Without seriously trenching upon either responsi- bility to Parliament or responsibility for the train- 10g, equipment and discipline of the army. But the Present dual system has the supreme disadvantage Of over-riding expert advice for political reasons,and then blaming the expert when deficiencies occur Which the expert has in vaia endeavoured to avert. Parliamentary control must be made more effective 13)- what will increase the effoctiveness of our finan- tial preparations. Army, Navy, and Civil Service "timates will have to be more closely examined by

cotamittees before they come before the House of Commons, and these committees will have to stand etween the Government and the experts and per- roanent officials by calling the latter before them in secret whenever they think doubts can be removed and explanations given. A searching examination is imperative, and it cannot be obtained under our present system, especially with the closure as a weapon of pressure and limita- tions as to time. The open committee must be reserved for general items. This double plan will Protect experts and preserve Parliamentary con- trol. The present plan gives Parliamentary con- trol in a loose way, and enables the Minister to overcome as well as to hide the espert. We must always haves Commander-in-Chief, but if we go O n limiting his powers and spreading responsibility over so wide an area we shall get the maximum of expenditure with the minimum of efficiency, end nobody will feel or exercise real responsibility.

It has escaped general notice that the . Lord Chief Justice made an unusual exercise of his dis- cretionary powers in the Bennett trial. Women Were excluded from the court. It can hardly be 44.1 d that this niarked the adoption of a new prac- ' ,toe, because it was possible that the defence ~ight have taken a turn which would have made the presence of ladies awkward. But counsel Would have given a hint if this were likely to be 40, and the broad facts were not such as to cause 4.115' discomfort to the other sex. Moreover, it is rid that Lord Alverstone had a letter-bag full of aktters every day from distinguished ladies and arir husbands begging that the privilege of a peep the prisoner might be allowed at any stage "t the inquiry. The truth was that prohibition Wa.s issued out of consideration for the Prisoner, and not out of regard for the feelings of so-called gentlewomen. These women have in the past infringed the code of decency by their insensate curiosity. They have used lorgnettes to stare at a wretched person tremulous with anxiety under his accuse- yon, and have aggravated his embarassment. It la only right that prisoners should be protected from critical dissection ()kills kind, and it will be held that the Lord Chief Justice was wise and humnoe in his action. The broad reason why the Public are'admitted to a court of justice is that these observers, by their presence, may assist in aceing that justice is done. Cynics who say that w.ernen cannot reason will affirm that their admis- s worse than useless ; but, on the other hand, the right is in ordinary cases due to them, in order that they may know that their sisters are properly treated by a tribunal, of judge and jury, consisting Solely of men. They have themselves to thank if that right is withheld.

Members of the new rifle clubs may be some- What interested in an appeal which has been addressed to them—and, indeed, to the marksmen Of all nations—to compete this summer in an inter- oational shooting match at Lucerne. The terms of the appeal are effusive, and the grammar of the nglish version more than doubtful ; but of the heartiness of the invitation there can be no doubt. The marksmen of all foreign countries are addressed s" dear friends," and are promised that if they Will attend at the Federal shoooting, from June 30th to July 11th, the greatest of Swiss national festivals, their hosts will do their best to make the "pleasant and honorific." There are other iOducements,of course offered to competitors in this "noble shooting trial" besides Swiss hospitality and the beauty of the Alps. They are told by the committee that, "guided by a lively conscience of our noble duty, we shrink back from no sacrifice Order to make the contest worthy of you." -c.orther, they are reminded tbat "beautiful prizes .Wait them," mad "then do not forget," the appeal continues, "our national shooting festival invites equally, endowed as it is with 800,000 francs, to excluding no foreigner, as far as he complkes the prescribed firearm." With the "Swiss Oplicity" of which mention is made, the Presi- L`eot and Secretaries inform the marksmen of every ,71ntry that "Lucerne expects them all !" The "wspapers are begged "kindly to propagate this 411," and we willingly do our share,for the benefit ..,, any who may be inclined to test their marks- toanship in the land of William Tell.

Many opinions have split 43,,11 the rock of the Government's war policy, and to ' e Liberal party forming the opposition has ap- vt''ared in recent times with a front far from un- broken in the face of the foe. The disaffection ;which undoubtedly existed has proved, however, „"°,,,he very limited in extent, and the irreconcil- "Th.ules were signally defeated at the mooting 'on Wednesday. They had formed the bold project °f capturing the Federation and securing the ascendancy for their own extreme views, but in- stead they have sustained a distinct set-back which unfeignedly rejoice over. They have identi- ,,"ll themselves with the Transvaal Committee, the uoneiliation Committee and kindred organisations Which have not come out of recent disclosures at all well, and in consequence have iuvited the snub eY got from delegates and members of the ederation who did not "wish the groat represen- twa.ttve organisation of the party to be identified ith the views and methods of these Committees oci their supporters "—to use the wording of an 04P_ Peal issued by representative delegates. div.head: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
A Provincial Letter.

I It is twelve months this week since his present Majesty delivered a tzreat speech at Bethnal Green on Workman's D ovellings ; and although no cognis- ance was taken in the King's speech at the opening of Parliament of the necessity of any reform of the laws relating to the housing ot the working classes, it is tolerably certain that the Government will yet make an w tempt to initiate legislation in that sense In all the large provincial towns and cities, as well as in the metropolis, the question has become urgent, and any honest endeavour to afford guidance towards a solution is acceptable. Mr. Balfour's somewhat utopian scheme of motor- cars running along specially construct:A caus,ways can be allowed to stand over in this connection for the present. His views are mainly philosophical, though it would be unwise to deny that the motor- car, when the production of that class of vehicle has become sufficiently cheap, may ultimately play a part in the se'tlement of the overcrowding difficulty. The chety tram and the cheap railway train are the agencies on which reliance may be more confidently placed for all present and practi- cal purposes. The mistake hitherto made in the administration of the existing Act is that too punc- tilious attention has been paid to those sections of it that require rebuilding on insanitary areas which have been cleared. As originally presented this proposition appear d simple enough; but many economic changes have occurred since that Act was passed, and the experiment of municipal building on cleared areas at the centre has proved all but a failure. So that it is towards cheap travelling facilities that the reformers are now largely direct- ing their attent ion, and where these do not already exist they have somehow to be pr ,vided.

The cry of" no politics "is heard at nearly every municipal election, and just as often when the day of polling arrives the cry is dropped. It is seldom, indeed that London can point the way for the pro- vinces in matters municipal, but it did so on Saturday There was absolutely iry room for doubting London's verdict at the list General Elec- tion London has been Conservative in Imperial matters since 1886, and never was so overwhelm- ingly so as in October last. All this seemed to point to a sweeping change in the constitution of the London County Council on Saturday; but, as a matter of fact, the result was in the opposite direc- tion. The Liberals, or Progressives,, completely swept the field. Conservative M.P.'s were rejected by their own constituents when asking for rnuni- cipal honours, and Liberal,' who were badly beaten at the polls in October, when standing for Parlia- ment, were n)w elected by large majoriti-s for the s ime division on the Dmnry Council election Urban District Councils and To vn Councils might with advantage take a hint from 31turday's London County Council elections,

That the camera cannot lie is a statement that had almost attained to a dignity of a proverb But perhaps no one knows better than the photographic expert that the veracity of the camera is not always unc mllengeable. Tricks of light and focus are re- sponsible for many awkward distortions of a picture. The camera employed by the beach artist at Yar- mouth in the recent murder case distinctly converted a link watch chain into one of a rope pattern, the change being mainly due to the per.on wearing the chain making a movement during the few seconds of exposure. But even in the hands of the most practised operator the camera is at to 'produce misleading effects on the negative, and the evidence on this point at the Yarmouth trial might inspire a volume of letterpress and pictorial examples of the freaks of photography. In a sense the camera is a ' detective, but it would be a serious mistake to argue, after recent disc weries, in favour of the camera's infallibility. So that the man in melo- drama who declares "the apparatus cannot lie." will have to reconsider his sweeping asseveration. Among the questions put forward in the House of Commons during the last few days, was one to the Home Secretary with reference to the captur- ing of small birds with fishing hooks, baited with worms, a discreditable practice said to be common in certain Cornish fishing villages It is hoped that so brutal a practice is not known to the youths of other counties The Home Secretary, who con- demned the practice,directed attention to the Wild Animals in Captivity Protection Act,l9oo, and said that, not knowing fully the particulars, he was not sure whether the offence came within the pro- visions of that Act, which, however, was passed tor the purpose of preventing such practices. Mr A Cross, M.P., who has interested himself in the matter, says that if sufficient facts to act upon are brought to the knowledge of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals steps will be at once taken to deal with the matter under the Act mentioned.

Railway travellers have received with a smile of incredulity the announcment that the London and North-Western Railway Company have introduced an alarm signal by which a passenger himself can stop the train. So many of these signals have been announced from the moment when the communica- tion cord was first condemned that the scepticism is, perhaps justified. A few months working, how- ever, will educe whatever there is of value in the invention. The most manifest drawback appears to be that to use the signal in question the pas- senger has to stand up, which, in many cases that have occurred was shown to be impossible. In France the chain is hung half way down the win- dow. and although that has not proved to be in- fallible, it is a question whether it is not worth a trial.

A good deal of discussion still centres in the ques- tion'of the new dietary scale for the various work- houses, and it has yet to be seen what part the proposal will play in the forthcoming elections of Boards of Guardians. But by that time the new rule will be in operation. Meanwhile the public are being informed by Guardians land their officials of the difference it will make in the cost of the food provided, chiefly in the diregtion of an increase. The increase in some Unions is expected to be .£3OO or more. Meals in these institutions should, if most of these reports be true, be apre appetising than they have been hitherto. A reverend gentleman, who is chairman of a committee of Guardians to which the dietary question had been referred, has discovered some curious facts in a study of the his- tory of Poor-law administration. Under the old regime, in the first quarter of the last century, he finds that one of the rules of a " celebrated" work- house was that every inmate might be helped as often as he pleased to roast beef or mutton on con- dition that he emptied " his plate each ti,te before coming again." In some workhouses, it was neces- sary that the paupers should eat their fare, but all that was over and above their appetite they ex- changed with the master for gin And this was prior to the advent of "Oliver Twist." The name of the narrator is suppressed here, but can he given frlf he were not entitled to the style iandecitiliedtilre";everend," one might be disposed to doubt the whole story, though the committee of which he was chairman did not.

The President of the Local Government Board has in dealin with representations on the Housing Question, rather damped the hopes of reformers by saying he does not consider the matter ripe for re- consideration by his Board.

FORTY-FITE CONVICTION'S IN THIRTY-ONE YEARS At Runcorn Police Court on Thursday, Messrs W Handley and E Imison, sentenced Sarah Dowd to three months hard labour for stealing a skirt, value Is,the property of Mary Jane Wilson.—The prisoner explained that she only borrowed the skirt, but when she returned on Saturday night the lodging. house was closed and she had to go elsewhere.— Superintendent Pearson said the prisoner although only 31 years of age, had 45 convictions recorded against her in Liverpool, St. Helens, and Warring- ton for a variety of offences.

On Saturday morning, before Mr S Brighouse, coroner, an inquest was held on the body of Peter Beesley, aged 68 years, at the Ball of Ditton. Toe evidence showed that the deceased's injuries were caused by falling downstairs on the 26th ult.—A verdict of accidental death was returned. INTERESTING TO RUNCORN Ole CONSUMERS

SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES. Mona Halliwell Heath, wife of John Heath, dolt gateman, 6, Ship-street, Widnes, was found dead at , her residence on Friday. It appears that Mrs. Heath during the last twelve months had been in a delicate state of health, and had been attended at intervals by Dr. Heatock, Widnes. The doctor granted a certificate to the effect that death wa the result of fatty degeneration of the heart. The Coroner does not deem an inquest necessary. DEATHS OF WIDNES Lams. Mrs. Keighlev, wife of Superintendent Keighley, of the Widnes Police Division, died at ten minutes Past nine on Saturday morning, at her residence in Victoria-road. The deceased lady had been ailing off and on all winter, and had been attended by Drs. William and Crighton Hutchinson. During the past two years she experienced a great deal of trouble, having lost her two sons. The funeral will take place on Tuesday. We have also to record the death of Mrs Barlow, wife of Coancillor Barlow, of Farnworth. Widnes. The deceased lady was taken suddenly ill at eleven o'cleck on Friday night, and died at a quarter past eight on Saturday morning. MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMEN. The Tuesday night concert at the above insti- tote was as successful as ever. The Chairman was lit H Wright. and a capital programme of musical items was provided. On Wednesday a service was held at which the Rev C E Stocks, Vicar of Widnes preached, and subsequently an organ recital was given by Mr W Grounds (organist of St Michael's Church) upon the organ which bas been transferred from St Michaels' to the Mission. Satisfactory col- lections were made in aid of the organ fund. SUCCESS OF A WIDNES CHOIR. On Saturday at the Earlestown Eisteddfod, the !vlersey Juvenile Choir, conducted by Miss Katie Thomas' secured the first prize. The adjadicator,Mr J B. Roberts, Mus . Bac , A.R.C.M., in giving his decision, said : "This choir has been splendidly trained, the expression and general rendering of the piece WWI excellent, and the choir thoroughly de- served the prize." Professor Ainsley was the accompanist. UNITARIAN LECTURES. , The Rev H D Roberts gave the first of a series of Four Lectures at the Public Hall, Runcorn, on Wed- nesday night to an interested audience. His subject was Free Religion, and he showed that the only re- ligion that was really free was that which strenu- ously maintaining its present belief, yet admitted that far more light, more truth was still to come from the God of all truth, the eternal source. On following Wednesdays at 8 o'clock, the Lecturer gives (2) Unitarians and the Bible, (3) Unitarians and Jesus. (4) The Gospel for the New Century. Every facility is given for questions and discussion, and the forty-five minutes thus occupied went with an excellent spirit. Lectures on the same subjects are given on Thursdays at Widnes in the Baths Hall at 8 o'clock.

div.head: LECTURE AT RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: LECTURE AT RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB.

The educational lectures at this club were resumed on Tuesday night last, when Mr. J M Frith gave an interesting paper on the Reform Bill and the Anti Corn Law Agitation. The struggles for the passing of thee two splendid measures, said the lecturer were the two great.st political fights of the 10th Century. The Reform Bill he claimed as the basis of all reform; and the Corn Law Bill was the forerunner of all those great measure which subse- quently aimed at removing the taxation from the necessities of the working classes. Mr. William Handley was the capable Chairman and there was a fair attendance. At the close of the paper there was an interesting debate.—The next lecture will be delivered by Mr, F J Norman 3.P., on Tuesday week. BLINDMISS. HYBSTGRT RESTOMCD.--DISBASEIS OP Titri

"Thu List Grip" and " Sing me a song of the South" were creditably rendered by Mr S Rawlins,while Miss M Collins sang very ably "Love's Old Sweet Song 'and "Daddy.' MURDBROUS ASS-AIILT WITH A UM JAR, Charles Bailey, a boatman, was brought before Messrs. Handley and Imison, at Runcorn Police Court on Thursday,charged with assaulting a youth named William Clare, who is employed as a horse driver by the Manchester Ship Canal Company. The prisoner pleaded guilty. The evidence showed that on Tuesday night the prisoner was under the in- fluence of drink and fell asleep on the settle in the drivers kitchen of the Dukes stables. When he awoke he went to the bedroom overhead and pulled one youth from bed and kicked him, and then struck Clare a savage blow on the forehead with a two lb jam jar inflicting a serious wound, P.C. Wilson,who rendered first aid said there was so much blood on the oed a pig might have been killed thers. There was a wound over Clare's left eye an inch long, and the eighth of an inch deep, from which he extracted three pieces of mug. There was also a wound over the left ear, within an inch of an artery and in a very dangerous position. , Evidence was given by the prosecutor, Stephen Rose and Walter Harvey, P.C. Wilson and P.C. Bowyer. The prisoner did not deny the attack, but alleged that he had great provocation. He said the youths threw cold water over him and filled his but with cinders and jam jars.—" The youths denied this statement. The Bench said even the provocation prisoner alleged did not justify him in making so brutal an attack upon a youth, and sentenced him to two months hard labour.
