div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, MARCH 8, 1901.
RE-OPENING OF THE HALTON-ROAD CHAPEL.

The re-opening of the Halton-road Chapel, Run- corn, for divine service will take place on Bunday next. The chapel has been altered structurally by the boiy of the chapel being literally lifted in alignment with the ceiling of the gallery ; thus forming a complete chapel with a schoolroom below. During the past few weeks the sacred building has been undergoing re-decoration at the hands of Mr James Green, painter, High-street, and the interior is now the most beautiful in the district. The schoolroom below also presents a charming appearance, being similarly decorated, but lending itself more unrestrainedly to the blending of the colours. The morning chapel, passages, and exterior have lalso been admirably attended to with a thoroughness deserving of the highest credit. _

MYiTRILIOIIS DROWNING CASH AT WIDNES. - On Saturday morning at the Whines Police Station before Mr S Brighouse, coroner, an inquest was held touching the death of Daniel Mclnerney, aged 21 years, who was found drowned in West Bank Dock, Widnes, on Wednesday afternoon, Mr Dodd was the foreman of the jury,—Thomas Mcln- erney, father of the deceased, residing at 16, Peel- Street, Widnes,said deceased lived with him, and he was a labourer at Bolton's Copper Works —lu reply to the Coroner, witness said not an angry word passed between them. He was stopped on the Saturday previous, but witness never knew that he was stopped until Monday morning. James Shakeshaft, saia that on Monday he was in the Waterloo Vaults,about seven o'clock in the evening. He saw the min Daniel Mclnerney in the hou,e with his uncle, John Lawler. He was smoking a cigarette. Shortly after he started crying. Wit- ness asked him what was the matter, and Lawler replied. 'The old chap has been cracking on to him, I expect.' Deceased said "He has driven two or three away, and he would have driven ma too if I had been big enough." He then got up and said ' He had not seen him since.—John Lawler, uncle to the deceased, said deceased told him he intended to go away in a boat called the Fair Trade that was lying in the dock laden with coal. In reply to the Coroner, P.C. Smith explained that the vessel waS lying about twelve yards off the embankment. The Coroner: Was the body found near to where the vessel was lying ?—P C Smith : About four yards off —Mr Dodd, foreman, said they were quite agreed that the death was purely acci- dental.—The jury were quite satisfied he had not taken away his life, bir, were quite clear that tie came by it accidentally.

div.p: RUNCORN i ES.

[BY A COURESPONDENT] The Runcorn School Board are giving cause of considerable annoyance to many Runcorn rate- payers, who object to sending their children to any but a Board School ;but, in so much, as there is no accommodation for the children in the Board Schools what else can the Sc'dool Board do but 'recommend that the children be sent to the Church Schools? They muit see that children are educated, and to the Board the course they are now pursuing seems the only way out of the difficulty.

That it isnot the only way out of the diffl laity has been partly proved by Mr William Ilandley,who advocated the advisability of attempting a little ad- justment of the Granville-street Schools, so that higher standards might be accommodated. True the Education department objects to any infringement of its regulations for the control of infant schools, and this is a fact Mr Fiandley takes care to em- phasise. But surely his contention that some ad- justment might be brought about is worth con- sideration ; and, the Board would be better advised, if they set about the work rather than institute proce-dings against ratepayers who have strong objactions to sending their children into Church Schools. At present the majority on the Runcorn Scho3l Board are representatives of the interests of Voluntary Schools. Yet, whilst the ratepayers have accomm xlation for some 100 children going to ab- solute waste in the Granville-street School, they should be careful not to display their hand too plainly, but rather accept the suggestion before "the cat is amongst the pigeons."

The Norley Parish Council is decidedly a unique body. On very reliable authority lam told that their Clerk receives no payment for his services,and that practically the Council is ruled by one man. Indeed, to such a pretty pass have things come,that at the annual Parish meeting, on Monday last, it was thought better that the Parish should have no Council at all, in preferenc; to the despotic rule of the one individual who has ruled the roost for them in the past; and a resolution to the effect that the Parish revert to the old state of things was actually passed by the meeting. That such a state of things should exist in the heart of enlightened Cheshire is deplorable.

TRH ADVANT&OES OF THE RUNCORN TECHHICAL 5C11001.9. Mr J Wilson, chairman of the Technical Instruction Committee, referred to tbs Cambridge University local examinations, and as to how the day students had fared at that examination. They had received the returns, end as could have been seen from the newspapers 16 Students had u,eoessfully passed the test. The result was an encouragement to the governing body, and to the staff, and showed clearly that the teaching given in the school was of a very satisfactory character. Toe value of technical education was admitted by every well-wisher of his country. He doubted Whether it occurred to some parents that it was ot great Importance for thir ir boys, after they had left the elementary school at the age of 12 or thereabouts, and who were going to be tradesmen or artisans, that there ahoul i be a further training in a science school for about three years before joining the Technical Instruction Classes, in order to triable them the better to grasp the instruction given in those classes, and make greater progress in their studies. He was afraid the thing that usually happened was, too many parents allowed those years to be wasted ; and as a consequence much of what had been learned at the elementary school, and which would, if followed up be of practical use in after days, was almost, if not ent rely, forgotten* They instituted the day school in the hope that parents would aid the young folk to continue their education so well begun in the elementary stage, and to pass on to the higher branches of education, and to the evening classes in the institute. It would be remembered that some of the members of the Council paid a visit to the recent Educal•ional Exhibit of the Uoited States of America, which had been brought over from the Paris Exoosition to the city of Manchester. That exhibit showed them the great advance made in education generally and in Technical Education in particular, by the United States, who were year by year becotning, one of England's greatest rivals in Foreign markets. By their new scientific methods recently developed te an enormous extent, they honed to secure the markets of the world for the manufacture of steel. He (Mr Wilson) hoped, however, they would not succeed in that; tan.if they did, it would be one of the greatest blows this country would ever receive. It behoved every parent , therefore to give his children the best scientific edu- cation they could. (Hear. hear.) Mr Imison supplemented Mr Wilson's remarks and pointed out the chief merit of the successes was in the indication that the Runcorn School Board whilst essenti- ally a science and arts (01°31, also taught history and literature so well.
The Chairman added the important fact that the students had sat for the examination without any special craramhag for the occasion. (Rear, hear).

div.head: NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS HORTICULTURAL SOCIETY. Annual Meeting.
div.p: NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS HORTICUL- TURAL SOCIETY. Annual Meeting.

The annual general meeting of this Society was held in the Town Rail, Newton-le-Willows. on Tuesday eves- ing. Mr J Randall presided, and amongst those present were : Meesrs A Smith, J Sephton, J Simm, T Foden, Lane, and T Williamson (secretary).— De minutes of the last annual meeting were read and confirmed. The statement of accounts showed the total receipts to be £64 54 1111, which included a balance of £l. 134 63 from 1.899. and subscriptions £39 2s 61. The expendi- ture was £53 lie 611, leaving a balance of £5 14s sd. On the motion of Mr A Smith, seconded by Mr W Seoliton, the balance sheet was adopted. The Chairman observed that the next question was the advisability of holding a show this year, and on that point be hardly knew what to say. The Secretary said the coming year seemed rather hopeful. Mr Moon had told him that he could not pos- sibly Attend the meeting, but he was willing to act on the Committee:if elected, and he would Ware them prizes to the amount of his prize money last year. Ho (the Secretary) had received a priz> from " Tit Bits " and " Pearson's Weekly." Mr Swift, ironmorwer, Earlestown, also promised to give one or two prizes. (Hear, hear.) Mr A Smith said it seemed to him they ought not to hesitate on the subject, and he would propose that they hold another show so long as they were able to pay their way, and supported as they were by a very numerous and influential list of subscribers, and so long as they continued to take an interest in the Society, he thought they ought to further their interests and carry on the I show. (Hear, bear.) I par Clough seconded and it was carried unanimously. On the motion of Mr Sephton and seconded by Mr Lane, the Patrons were re-elected.

Me A Smi'h was re-apininted Hon. Treasurer. In thanking them for their confidence he said he did not think there wag any Society in the District that was more worthy of support than ths Horticultural Society. Ile did not consider there was anything had a greater influence upon them than the pursuit of Horticulture and the more they cluld cultivate it amongst them the better it would be.

The next business being the election of Secretary, Mr Williamson said he wished to resign the position. He found he could not carry it(fon as it ought to be, his various duties preventing him. Mr A Smith proposed that Mr S Randall should be appointed to the officeatie thought he would be able to perform the duties which were arduous, and which would occupy a considerable amount of time, but he would have the benefit of his father's assistance in the condunt of the affairs of ths society. Mr Foien seconded, and the motion was unanimously adopted. The following were elected the Committee of Manage- ment :—Messrs J Randall, T Woods, R Anderson, J Baker, T E Clough, T Roden, W Lane, Joseph Owen, J Roscoe, W S,phton, C Siriltl3, Craven, Sandiford, and Moos:

The chairman proposrd a vote of condolence with Mrs. Kitchen on the death of her husband, who was a mem her of the committee and a most energetic worker and he knew he was only expressing the feeling of the corn- mitres when he ssid they sympathised with her in the gr,at loss she had sustained.

- Mr. Lane Rpconcipd. Mr. A Smith supported and said ha was sure they had suffered a great loss in the death of Mr Kitchen, whereby one of their earliest supporters had been removed, and they could not do other to mark their sense of the loss than by passing the resolution. A vote of thanks to all the donors of prizes and others who had givpn any assistance at the past year's show was accorded. A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the pro- ceedings;

div.head: Personal.
div.p: Personal.

Among the candidates who successfully passed the London Matriculation last January was Miss Margaret Pierrepant Banks, a granddaughter of the late Mr. Thomas Banks, of Warrington.

div.head: WORKINGMEN AND THE INFIRMARY. Annual Meeting of the Workingmen's Cornmittee.
div.p: WORKINGMEN AND THE INFIRMARY. Annual Meeting of the Workingmen's Cornmittee.
Mr. Monks and the Feathers Hotel.

There was a representative attendance at the annual meeting of the Workinimen's Committee of the War- rington Infirmary and Dispensary, held in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall, on Saturday afternoon. The Mayor occupied the chair. There was a large attend- ance, which included Mr F Monks, Mr John Roberts (chairman of the Working Men's Infirmary Committee), Mr J L Tunstall (hon. treasurer), and Mr Joseph Taylor (bon secretary). Several of the hon. medical officers of the institution were also in attendance. MR DOWN AND THIS ATTENDANCE AT THE CONCERT. Thea Bore. SECRETARY read letters of apology for non- attendance from tdr Charles White and Mr Thomas J Down. The latter, in the course of a long letter, said : —" You are quite aware how greatly I appreciate the noble work done by your committee and yourself, and I stneerely hope and trust that your efforts to benefit the Infirmary and kindred institutions may meet with con- tinued and increasing success. I was sorry to see so many empty 'front' seats at the concert. Cannot some- thing b 3 done to &fist the sympathy and support of those for whom they are specially provided ? At present they are remarkably conspicuous by their absence from the entertainments you provide, and the melancholy array of empty stalls must b 3 somewhat depressina, I snoulci say, to the performers, and a serious loss to you. ' Is it because the concerts are not advertised in the news- papers,or is it because the general public think that as it is a working men's affair it is certain to be low and rowdy? If the latter, it is a pity the truth cannot he brought home to them. I have had a long experience of the concerts arranged by your erommittee,and can personally testify that the audiences are as orderly and well behaved as anyone could wish them them to be. It has also occurred to me that there may be some persons who would prefer to hear some other band than mine. I have had the honour (which I greatly value) of being associat- ed with your concerts for a considerable number of years and am as willing as ever to do anything I can for you, but if a change of band would be an ad litional attrac- tion to the persons I have referred to, do not let any consideration for me stand in the way. I desire to see your work prosper, and I am anxious that your com- mittee should feel perfectly free to adopt th, course which in their opinion is b-s; adapted to promote that object. You can read this letter to the meeting if you think it desirable to do so."

MR MONKS AND THE LICENCE OF TRE FEATHERS HOTEL. The following letter was also read from Mr. Monks, who was prosent at the meeting :—"Walton OH flail, near Warrington. 25th February, 1901. Mr Joseph Taylor. D beg to acknowledge your Inter of th- 23rd, and shall have great pleasure in attending the meeting on Saturday next at 3.30. You will have noticed that the Corporation are iniending to rebuild the Feathers Inn in Bridge-street, and it has occurred to me t ) snzgest wh, tly,r your committee would care to be- c Jule the holder of the liaence,and put in a suitable man- ager, who should have no pecunia-y interests in the sale of beer, Sze- It is not a tied house and, of course, you could buy pure lo.cTr and sell it at a profit, which should go to asAlst your funds for the Infirmary. It IS an experiment I think well worth trying, and it could be ventilated on Saturday when the Mayor is present. Yo, mighs get many members intereqted and have good attendancE, so that the subject wcu'd be well con- sidered, and, if thought desirable, the new c ommitt.e could be iastru:tod to take it Up.—Yours faithfully, F. Moen."
TIM HON TIIELI3IIIIEII.B STA.TEMENT.

The Hot( fas&SUBSR made a financial Waiement with reference to the contributions to the institu-lon. The total a nount received for the veer per the Workinv C marnittee was £1,169 13 3P, expenses £32 16, 10p, leaving £1,136 4s 51. The cycle re Arade aid carnival and watch coemetition realised £365 2s 9J, the Infirmary concert £45 13153, and the police sports £23 31. From a printed statement with regird to the sub- scriptions to the Warrington and District Nursing Asioc ation for the year 1900, per the Working Men's Committee, it appeared that the amount handed to the treasurer of the asseciation was £67 111 6d. In each ease the printed statement of accounts were signed by Mr J L Tunstall (hon treasurer) and Mr C Jackson Holmes (bon auditsr). In his statement with regard to the contributions per the Working Men's Committee to the Infirmary Mr Tunstall said that he hoped that with the help of the cycle parade funds and with the Increased subscriptions by the Working Men's Com- mittee their adverse balance on the deficiency revenue amount of £1,140 ought to be reduced to nearly £590 during the current year. He hoped the gentlemen who got up the cycle parade would repeat their efforts during the current year. (Hear, hear.) If so, he had considerable hope of wiping off their adverse bilance altogether by the end; of next year. The subscriptions . in themselves amounted to £678, which was juit the equivalent of the highest amount they had ever received from the Working Men's Committee,including all sources of income, and that was exceedinzly creditable. At the same time he hoped the Committee would put forth their best efforts to still further increase the amount. The town was growing, new works were being erected in every direction, old works were being considerably extended, and that meant that they would have many more cases of accidents. It would, therefore, be abso- lutely necessary within the next two or three years that they should again'extend the building, and in that ease their income would be deficient unless they could find out some means of increasing it. The work of the VVorkingmee's Committee was considered by everyone to be exceedingly creditable. (Hear, hear.)

A LICENSING EXPERIMENT. Mr. MONKS, in moving the adoption of the accounts, alluded to the increased subscriptions, and said he thought they might do even still better in the future. He hoped it might not prove to be an untrue prophecy that I they would make the amount of the submription £1,500 some of these days. (Heir, hear and applause.) There was some satisfaction, on looking at the balance sheet, to find that considerable iaterest was taken in some of I the works, the subscrintion from which had been con- siderably increased. Tnose works were mentioned.' The Isame increase would apply to all the works if th .re was WAGE individual to be found who would make it his busi- ness to work up the collections as they had been worked up in the works he bad mentioned. It was all a matter of oreanization, and he was sure it would be quite as I easy for the amount to be increased to £1,500, as it had been to raise it to a little over £l,OOO. The co-operation of the employers was also required, because they could help very much indeed. (Hear, hear.) He expressed his thanks for the assistance given to the Nursing Asso- ciation, which required an increased subscription. because instead of having four nurses, Vier had now six fully employed. They required £603 a year to meet their expenditure. Be expressed his satisfaction to find that , the total amount of the subscriptions to the Infirmary had reached £1,136 4s 51. He saw from the newspapers that the Vicar of St. Paul's had broached the question of the Feathers Ho`el licence ; it was not exactly his (me Monks's) idea, but something similar. The Rev John Yong° had also- writtea to the press on the same subject, but more with a view of suppressing the liceece altogether. In the works he (the speaker) had charge of in Csalbrook-dale, in Shropshire they had had considerable annoyance from a public-house adjoining the works. It belonged to them and he had given the tenant notice to qnit. He in- tended that that public-house should serve as an experi- ment. He would put it in charge of the work men,and they would be responsible for its management. It would f erm a very comfortable and cenvenient nucleus for the I men's clubs, and whatever profit was made would go to I their own rasources. (Applause.) He was talking to the manager about the matter last week, and be suggested that it should form the RUCiPUS of a pension fund; he had not the slightest objection to anything that would tend to make the people more independent and it I should be quite understood that the experiment was not I that the men were to make themselves drunk and abuse the privileges, but get reasonable refreshments and be able to buy pure beer. Altogether he let that it would be a very successful contribution to, any fund which might be started—either pension or sick fund. (Hear, hear.) The Feathers Hotel belongad to the Warrington Corporation, and if the Working Men's Committee chose te take the matter in hand he did not see wLy the plan he had sketched should not be satisfactorily worked in Warrington. At any rate it was an experiment in the right direction, because, say what they would, men would please themselves whether they were teetotalers or not. Toe successful plan was to meet all reasonable and rational recreation in a reasonable and proper way. Ihe Feathers Hotel could form the basis of an interest- ing experiment which would be a benefit to working men, and more particularly to the institution in which they were all interested. (Applause.) Mr Crosskill seconded the motion for the adoption of the accounts and it was carried. THE MAYOR'S OPINION.

The MAYOR then addressed the meeting at length, and expressed the pleasure it afforded him to see such a large, influential, and representative body of working men, especially because the object of the meeting was such an excellent one. The position of Mayor of a town like Warringten imposed a great amount ef work upon the holders of the office, and there were some duties one would be pleased to be relieved of, but not having much opportunity of rendering practical service to the institution he was glad to take charge of the meeting, and to say a few words as to its claims, and the splendid manner in which they had been met by this organized attempt to raise sub-. scriptions. During the year no fewer than 624 in patients bad been treated, of whom 391 were males and 233 were females t. and when he reminded the meeting that out of that total there had been no fewer than 337 accident cases it spoke volumes to the necessity of ample provision being made in a manufacturing town for cases where immediate treatment was necessary if life was to he saved. The increase of the total number of cases was 57. In addition to the treatment of cases in the institution itself during the year 1,096 persons had been treated in their own homes ; 2,477 patients bad come to the Infirmary for medicine and advice, and

2.406 accident and emergency cases had been treated making the large total of 5,979 cases. Ttoese figura were eloquent in themselves, and needed no enlarge- ment on his part. Now, as to the manner in which the responsibility of the working men bad been discharged. At, they knew, the maintenance of the wives and children of the men doing their duty in South Africa on behalf of King and country had laid an additional burden on the town, which had been most nobly met by all classes, and by none less nobly than by the workingmen themselves. Speaking as a native of the town, and as one who had gone through the various grades in all matters, he-could say that where thoughtfulness and jkiadliness of heart were needed the working people of the town—men and women—had been second to none with regard t.O what , had been done in other towns in the United Kingdom. (Hear, bear.) Prior to the organization of the Working Men's Infirmary Committee, the sub- scriptions for a period of ten years amounted to £734 is 80, or an average per annum at £73 83 21. Taking the year 1880 as the first year in which the committee was organised; the sub- scriptions amounted to £lB5 19s 4d, but the total from that year up to 1900 had reached the large sum of £10,207 143 81 or an average for the last 21 years of just close upon £5OO a year—a most creditable and sat- lafactory result. (Applause.) He la Med to emphasize ' the reference of Mr Tunstall to the excellent resulta of the Cycle Parade. He felt grateful to those who : rendered assistance on that occasion, and he hoped the remarkable success of last year would be reneated for many years to come. (Applause.) Mr Monks had furnished him with a topic which, if be chose to occupy their time, he could speak to them about for the whole of the afternoon. Be was afraid that before the ques- tion of the Feathers Hotel was alsolutely and finally settled they would get a good many recommendations as to what was the best way to deal with it. The meet. lag knew where he was on the question. Hr should have beea very glad to have done with it altogether by leaving it alone, but be was in a minority upon that subject. Ile did not know whether the Council would be disposed to allow the licence to be held by some one connected with the Working Men's Committee for the purpose which had been suggested by Mr Meaks,but they might dos great deal worse. If the house was to be occupied as a public-house, with a suitable restric- tion, and with a man in charge having no personal Interest in inducing his customers to take more drink than was good for them, the profits after the payment of eapenses might perhaps be disposed of with as great an ad eantageto the committee for purposes of the Infirmary as any other object. (Applause.) However, at that very early stage of the consider.tion of the qneßtien—and it was going te be rather e thorny one—it was impos- sible to suggest in what light the Council m :ht take the proposition of Mr Monks, but he would promise the meeting that the matter should have very careful serious, and unprejudiced consideration when it came befare the Corporation to deal with in a practtal shape, Whether the committee became the honourable succ.ssors of the present Town Clerk in the holding of the licence—(laughter)—if it was possible to utilize the establishment for such a noble object, so far as his influence was concerned it abould be used in that dime tion: (Hear, hear, and applause.)

ELECTION OF OFFICERS. Mr NIGHTINGALE proposed the re-olection of Mr John Roberts, as chairman. He said he was opposed to the Wgrkiag Men's Committee having anything to do with the Feathers' Hotel ; he wouldt ike to see the experiment carried out by people who thought thes could make it a RUCCO99. Be suggested, however, that 'the committee should take tho Parr Hall for a series o!: Saturday evening concerts not high class concorts, but conceits with plenty of rollicking music %WWI WOUIC: make them laugh after a hard week's work. He greatly appreciated the music supplied by Mr Down's band, and he expressed a hope that the Nursing As.ociation would be supported. A home of its own should be provided, and there should he no ne-cessity to rent a houso. Councillor Rl:tarot; seconded, and the motion was carried.

Councillor Jorns ROBERTS suitably returned thanks. Mr D Fanshaw was, no the motion ni M" DAINTITE seconded by Mr CROSSKILL, re-elected deputy chairman: Mr FANRRAW, in reply, remarked that the deputy had very little to do and his office was an easy one as a rule, although of late more responsibility had devolved upon him owing to the increase of the funds through the exertions of their cyclist friends and of the football clubs. It was always a pleasure to him to do what he o:.uld for be institution. (ApplausP). Mears J L TIINSTALL and .1 TAYLOR were elected bon treasurer and ho n secretary respectively. The meting concluded with the usual votes of thanks,

div.p: THE 20TH CENTURY.

Do you know that it has cf ten been said that great events happen at the end and at the beginning of a Century ? No doubt we shall have the usual prophets forecasting the nrobabilities of all sorts of startling occurrences to mark the commencement of the 20th Century, but there is no one bold enough to predict that there will be less of pain and suffering, less of human misery and disease in the World. div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
EARLESTOHN COLLIERS' ADVI THEFTS.
-IIIPIIDENT

At the Warrington P‘.dice Curt on Monday, before Mr. F. Monks and other magistrates, Bridget O'Brien, whose address was given as 28, Dial-street, was charged with stealing from toe person of Ralph Hart, some time between 9 arid 9.30 p.m. on Saturday, a silk handker- chief and 9.1. in money, and also with stealing from the person of Henry Conroy, in a house in Dial-street, at 10 o'clock, the sum ot 2s 6.l.—She pleaded not guilty.—The Chief Constable said the prosecutors were colliers resid- ing in Errlestown, and they came to Warrington on Saturday night on " a little bit of • spree." In Scotland- road they were accesteel by the prisoner and an ex-con- vict named Fleming. Alter sense conversation prisoner snatched a silk handkerchief from Hart's coat pocket and walked away. The man pressed far the return of the handkerchief but the woman simply laughed at him. The prosecutors then proceeded to the " Travellers' Rest" Inn,Fennel-street,and the women followed them. They seemed to have entered into conversation and the prisoner claimed relationship witti Conroy. She invited them to come to her sisters' house in Del.-street. Being strangers to the town they knew not Dial-street and went with the prisoner and Fe,ming. At the house they found another woman and a number of men, and the prosecutors were asked if they could contribute towards providing refreshaint for the company. Hart pulled 91 from his pocket and it was immadiately snatched from him by the prisoner. He attempted to remonstrate with her, but was iotimidated by the men bullies who sat around. Conroy, under preisure, pulled out 2 81 and this was als.s snatched by toe prisoner. The prosecutors then commenced to demand the return of the money and handkerchief and they were immediately set upon by the other men and bundled into the street. They made a complaint to the police and P.C.'s Lewis and Hayes apprehended both the women. As Fleming had not taken any part in the theft, she was allowed to go. , The prisoner was a notorious character, and recently frequent complaints of the ['lnning of drunken men had been made.—The magistrates committed the prisoner to goal for three montras. Prisoner; I can do that. It won't . kill me.

Half-a-d( Z2(l smad hoys named James Smith, 37, Plumpton-street ; Joeeph Shaw, 39, Plumpton-street Charles Chadwick, 160, Liverpool-road; William Farmer 162, Liverpool-road ; Alfred Rankin, 397, Liverpool- read ; and Ambrose Timmins; 7, Plumpton-street ; were summoned before the Warriegron ms,:istrates on Mon- day for committing a bietch of the peace in Liverpoal- /road by acting in a disorderly manner on the 22:id oil-- Thomas Connolly, a 'bus conductor, residing at 10, Orford-street, stated that at 6.30 p.m. on the date in question he was cnnducting the 'bus which ran from antrey Bridges to Warrington. In Liverpool-road, he was set npon by a gang of boys including the defendants who tried to get on the step of the'bus.He prevented them from doing 90, and they commenced to strike him with sticks, throw muo at him, spit in his face and call him "injurious names." He complained to the 'hus inspec'or about their conduct and th,s matter was reported to the police. He had been annoyed by lads on previous occasions.—P.C. Woods alQo gave evidence.—On being asked what he had to say, Smith told the magistrates that they hit the 'tree conductor with sticks because he "stuck up for the Bons.'.— The Chi.f Constable: Vindi- cating the honour or the Empire. (Laughter)—The boy Rankin denied having assaulted the 'bus conductor and said he was only running along the footpath.—The Chief Constable: Loading, his morel support—The Chairman said the Bench were sorry that they could not let the boys have a taste of wlist they gave the 'bus conductor. It would do thorn more good than anything else. Defendants would be bound over to keep the peace and ordered to pay the cysts (ss. each).

Death of Mr David Baillie Warrington. We regret to report the death of Mr David Baillie, which took place at his residence, 11, Frog- hall-lane, on Saturday at 4.30 a.m. The deceased gentleman retired from active employment at Christmas last, and shortly after the advent of the new year:he was:seized with a paralytic stroke,from which he appeared to be recovering when a second but much more severe stroke occurred. Mr Baillie gradually declined and, being unable to take any nourishment, rapidly sank. He was 67 years of age and unmarried. His sister and he lived together, and this lady has been most attentive to him, spa.- ing neither time nor strength in trying to bring about his recovery. Dr Curtis was the medical attendant, and gave every care to his patient. Mr Baillie, was a native of Shandon, near lielensburgo, and came to Warrington nearly 40 years ago to the office ot Messrs James Fairclough and Sons. A little later he was appointed cashier with Messrs Armit- age and Rigby, of Cockhedge Mills, and hare he remained until eleven weeks ago, when declining health suggested a more restful time. On his , leaving the company Mr S R Armitage presented him with a batiaome watch and chain, the former bearing a suitable inscription and his monogram. It was hoped that he would have a long time to live and enjoy the provision made for his later days which he had intended to spend at his native place. For many years Mr Baillie was correspondent and treasurer of the once very flourishing Cockhedge Infants school. He leaves a brother and sister to mourn his loss. Prior to the depaiture of the rela- tives find the remains on Tuesday morning, the Rev John Yonge conducted a short service at the house, the company including Mr S 11 Armitage. Ihe funeral took place on Wednesday at Row, near lielensbtirgb.

The Wigan forwards then played with great judgment. and Eckersley was given an opening for further im provement. Runcorn defence stood the test, and Walker headed a rush for Wigan line. This was,however stayed by Prescwte securing another timely mark. Farmer marked near the centre, and Jolley this time landed a beautiful goal. Settling down with creditable vigour Wigan forwards secured scrummage after scrummage, and enabled Nelson and Rigby to dribble dangerously near the Run- corn line. Buttemorth saved just in time. With ad- mirable dash Runcorn then carried the leather back, and forced the Wigan defenders to concede a (lead-ball. This was bet a commencement of a number of attempts to break through, and Dickenson had an anxieus time, until Nelson secured temporary relief by a useful dash. Another series of attacks on the Wigan line followed, and Jolley dropped a goal from right un- der the posts. Wigan defence was good and at tbis stage the game was a pleasure to watch. Time and again the Wigan forwards got away with the,ball,at their feet, but Houghton was always more than enough to cover his line, and send them back again. The pressure on the Wigan defence was again at its height when Jacky Faulkner gave Jolley an opening and the first try was scored. Jolley's kick at goal however failed. Jones then carried play from the centre to Wigan 25, where Walker got possession and scored a daisy try. At half- time the SCE/re stood:—Runcorn, 2-2-10 ; Wigan, 0-0-0. When the game reopened it was noticed the wind had considerably dropped. Runcorn at enc.! pressed and from first to last, never gave their opponents a chance. Houghton was good and played with the coolness and dash of assured victory. Richardson scored the first try, but though in a good position Jolley failed to convert, floe borne forwards showed a marked im- provement and heeled out repeatedly with the result that Jolley and Faulkner were able to put their backs on splendid attacking tactics. As the result of bewilder lug passing, Jones, Butterworth and another fairly walked through the Wigan defence, and as Dickinson came down to retrieve the situ scion Jones passed to Butterworth and asked him to score. This Jimmy did with such effect tom Jolley could not miss adding the no,jor points. Right on to the finish Runcorn had the be4t of affairs, th- game ending :—Runcorn, 3 goals, 4 tries, 18 points ; Wigan, nil. Whitehaven v Widnes.

At Whitehaves, in a continuous downpour. The first half was cbsely contested, neither scoring. White- htven had tine best of the play. In the second half Westmoreland, of Whitehaven and Aspey were sent off the field. Hughes scored a clever try, Batey failing, at goal. Fir:tali—Widnes 1 try (3 points),to Whitehaven nil. Goole v St. Helens. Goole entertained the St Helens organiz stion on Satur- day before a go d muster of spectators. Miserable weather prevailed, and this militattd against good play. The visitors won the toss, and elected to play with a strong wind in their favour. Goole were penalised after ten minu•eh' play, and Hunter kicked a goal. St Helens kept up the pressure, and Campbell made a fatal mistaae tor Goole, allowing Pennington to score a soft, unconverted try. Goole next bad a turn of attack- ing, and Greeositt just failed to score a try. Before half time St Helens increased their score by another penaity goal. In the second moiety Goole attacked, and Cal- vert opened their account by a neatly dropped goal. By a good dribble, however. Green got through thit opposi- tion and t•cored a try for St Helens under thli posts Pennington this time converted. Ths play was very keen and exciting up to the finish, but nothing further was scored, the result being :—St Helens, 12 points ; , Goole, 2 points.

div.head: Fine Performance by Warrington at Leeds.
div.p: Fine Performance by Warrington at Leeds.
First Round.

The draw for the Northern Union Cup gave both War- rington and Leeds au excellent piospect, for the wie- ner of the enetch Newsreel" the two was so fortunate as to be at home to all visitors until the Bmi-finsl. Both clubs were, therefore, very keen on winning and as heeds were playing at Headingley the odds seemed sligtudy in their layout though Warrington had much the better record, Iu fact, tne visitors were fairly cot- lideut ot victury,and being backed by quite a thousand supporters they tripped on a heel more like a swamp man anything else, with helps of nerve. Rain was tailing in torrents and the wind blowing " great guns " straight down the fluid. Leeds had one or two absentees, J Coleman being unable to turn out at centre, and Ross, I forward. Warrington bad their selected team which in- cluded Dickenson as substitute for Elockenhall, who was injured the previous Saturday. 'fhere was a good gate, considering the weather, quite 8,000 spectators be- ing present, and the receipts amounted to £ll3. The referee was Matobinsun of Ulverston, and the teams lined out at 3.30 in tne following order : Warrington : Ilaiiam, lull back ; Fish, Isherwood, Dickenson, and Harria,teret quarters; R Bate and Duck- worth, halves ; Boerdinan, Morrison, Edmondson, Fell, Schoitz;Edeu, 8 sift, and Cunningham, forwards. L-eus : Jagger, tud back ; Coleman, Varley, Jackson and Bentley, threequertars; Daltry and Bogg,haif backs; Crowther, Matins, Sowden, Hanson, Harrison, Westmor- demi, I...iycock and Taylor, forwards. Warrlegton lost the toss and had to face the gale in the firs: half. Swift started and Warrington immediately entered Leeds territory, Duckworth and Bate getting away from the first scrimmage, the former making a fine run and passing forward to Harris. Bentley kicked strongly with the wind, but Harris fielded well and pu- in a good return. Another long punt from touch forced Warrington to concede a minor. Leeds worked their way to the Warrington quarter but Duckworth cleverly removed play to centre. B ate secured, put in a snor, kick whicu Harris followed no and drove the homesters back. Jagger returned powerfully, however,and Hallam miss-kicked the slippery ball which slid along the mud right under the feet of the Leeds forwards. The latter had a glorious chance of scoriog but Taylor spoiled it by attempting to pick up and knocking on. Warrington were haid pressed at this stage, Hallam several times failmg to reply to kicks which sent the ball in at a great speed. The tackling was very keen and this kept Leeds at bay, a clever mark by Bate in the thick ot me opponeets also coming in useful. Warrington gradually repelled the in- vasion, Isherwood leading the way to the home half with a dashing run. Dickenson replied effectively to Jaggeee puot and th! Leeds custodian was collared by Morrison close in. Isherwood passed to Fish but the latter was hemmed in and Jackson brought him down. Once on the attack,however, and Warrington shewed themselvi s much the smarter team. Rate and Duckworth passed smartly, the-latter beating everybody but Jagger who held him on the line. Leeds finally got to the quarter flag by a forward rush, but Warrington got poase44)n again and a series of qd ck transfers between the becks completely beat the opposition, Fish scoring cleverly at the earner amid frantic cheering from the Warrington spectators. The scorer failed at goal. From the drop- out Leeds followed up splendidly and Hallam was : tackled near the line. Bate lot offside and Varley took a penalty kick, just tipping the ball to his wing who was bowled in touch by Fish. Jagger tried at goal from a mark be Sowden but was uneuccessful. Warrington soon worked their way to the centre where Eden came under the ban of the referee for using more energy than wee required with Varley. He got off with a caution, and Warrington continued to hold Leeds in check. The home backs kicked strongly with the wind, but Warrington defended securely, Fish several times neatly clearing the line on the left. Twice Leeds grl under the posts through mistakes by Hallam, but each tires Duckworth got the ball and broke through in nut, style. Jackson was hurt and left tbe field a few minutes before the interval, when the score was Warrington, one try,; Leeds, nil.

-Varley resumed hostilities, Warrington failing to reply to the kick. Tne vbitors soon showed their line of action, however, and getting possession at the scrim- mage the whole of the backs passed beautifully aad ran well down into the Le, ds half. Jagger was tackled on the line and the case of the bomesters appeared deeper. ate la the extreme as the rain had ceased and Warringtnn handled the ball with astonishing accuracy. Jackbon returned to the Leeds ranks just as Fish got clear and the wing man appeared to 111191 a try through mistaking Jackson for a player before he had got on side. d. icon was not long in coming, for Bate, Duckworth, Dickenson and Isherwo,n corn bind so well that I...eds were demoralised, bihcrwood dashing through and scoring almost behind the posts. Fish kicked a goal. It was clearly now a question of what score Warrington would run up, as they overplay- ed Leeds at every point. Fish was off the field for some minutes changing his apparel, and in the meantime Leeds reached the centre. They were quickly repulsed by Duckworth, who fielded the ball under difficulties,and punted well into the home half. Here Jagger was slow, and Fell charged his kick down,scoring a good try under the posts, which the referee aisallowed. Warrington were operating at the quarter line and Bate tipped the ball across to Duckworth, wbo dribbled the ball splen- didly past man alter man, and finally kicked across for Harris to score an easy try. Fish failed at goal. Warrington maintained a hot attack, and after One Cr two combined movements had been checked, Fish got hold in front of the posts and wal,z-d round Jagger in his best style, afterwards placing a goal. There was no respite for the Leeds men who were quite outclassed,and just before time Bate bluffed the home halves and Fish again goaling. Final : dodged over near the pots, Warringten, three goals five tries (21 points) ; Leeds, tail.

" Dear Sirs.—l have been a great sufferer for dem on thirty years from my kidneys and stomach, and during that:time I have been frequently r.onficied to my bed for a month At a time—being compelled to lie on my back, in fact, unable to lie in any other position, the pain being so intense that I got little or no sleep night or day. div.head: Letter to the attor.
div.p: Letter to the attor.
_ Runcorn School Board and Granville
Street School.

See—Hiving read the report of the School Board Meedne of last week, I am afraid the mitotic will nt b 9, able to get a very clear conception from that report of the matter before the Board, re accommodation at Gran- Schools. As a parent who is affected by the driving away of children from these schools, I consider I have a right to give the pubic a few more details than are given them in a report of the Board meeting; Abr iat three weeks ago, my boy together with other boys, was sent away from these schools, because the Insee-ctor considered them too old for an infant school Their ages varied from 1 to 8 years. my boy being 71 years old. In the ordinary course of things they would have been drafted to the senior boys schdol at Victoria- road. In this case however that course could not be fol- lowed the school beiag already overcrowded. After vatic us enquiries, made by those in authority,room was found for them at the Trinity Schools. Several parents objected to these schools, and again search was made, with the result that room was found at the National Schools. This satisfied the requirements of some parents, tut still there were those left who ob- jected to any but a Board School Education for their children. This produced a deadlock, and my boy stayed at home. As the result of his non-attendance at school I was summoned before the School Attendance Commit- tee last Tuesday evening, and told that if I did not send him to school I should be prosecuted. You will see that the case stood thus. That I must either eei d him to these schools, to which I objected, or to none at all. I chose the latter with the result of threatened legal pro- ceedines. I consider that with thus threatening me with legal proceedings, the Board are acting very un- justly. The difficulty has arisen through their own shortsightedness, and it is hard indeed that I should suffer through their mistakes of the past. On making enquiries Ifind that if the Board would have spent a few pounds more on sanitary arrangements at Granville street schools, and have applied for permission to the Educational Department, to teach the lower standards of a senior boys school there, they would have avoided the difficulty which has arisen, and have eased the already overcrowded schools at Victoria-road. What is it to the ratepayers that certain schools in the town are not filled, and consequently will earn less for their managers than they would if filled ? How can Ibe expected to send ' my boy to these schools and thus help to earn a large grant for them, when I have no voice whatever in their management? There are schools in the town in the management of which, as a ratepayer, I have a voice, and I consider it my duty to send my children to these schools and earn a larger grant for them, and thus whilst getting for them the very best education, help to beep down the expense to the town for their mainten: ance It is a sorry thing for the ratepayers of Runcorn to remember that there is room for 130 more children at Granville-street schools, yet through the false economy of the Board in refusing to spend a few pounds more on the sanitary arrangements of the yard, they must lose a large amount in grants every year that would come to them, if these children were taught at Granville-etreet. It is high time that the ratepayers of Runcorn thought more of the welfare of their children in educational matters. than a paltry copper or two increase on the rates. We can never hope to overtake the Germans and Yankees in educational matters, until we throw overboard the policy of reckoning the cost before we launch out. May the time speedily come when a thinking population shall demand the very best education for their children, without considering whether it shall result in a rise or fall of the rates. Yours Sm. T SAUNDERS. 13, Brackley-street, Runcorn.

div.head: LATEST NEWS. Attack- on the German Emperor. –
div.p: LATEST NEWS. Attack- on the German Emperor. -
His Majesty Injured..
BR.EMEX, Wednesday.

While the E-nperar was driving from the Rathskeller to the railway station, a man named Dietrich Weiland, said to be a workman, threw a piece of iron at the Imperial carriage. Re was immediately arrested. The missile struck his Majesty under the right eye. The man Weiland after he was ar- rested had an epileptic attack. He is appar- ently of unsound mind. An official bulletin states that the wound is one and a half inches long and penetrates to the bone.

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS. Lichtenburgh Attacked by Delarey. Fighting all Day.
The War Ofd; has issued the following from Lord Kitchener : Pretoria. March 6th, 7.40 p.m. Lichtenburgh is being attacked by Delarey's forces. Fighting continued all day.

Arriving at 59, Cedar-street. I was ushered into an office where the click of typewriters told me that this was a busy department. In a few minutes I was intro- duced to Mr. VENO, a gentleman of medium height, 'dean shaved, with a clerical appearance, but active, earnest and full of business. My tale told, I was then shown the bottling and labelling department,which was a model of cleanliness. About a dozen girls with white aprons on were seated at long tables, labelling and wrapping VENO'S LIGHTNING COUGH CURE and VENO'S SEAWEED TONIC. "Have you a larga sale for the Lightning Cough Cure "I asked. "Yes, we are sending out thousands of bottles every week. It is sold by nearly all chemists and Co-operative Stores. I pride myself on having the most successful Cough Cure on the market ; that accounts for the large sales. It differs very much from the common, syrupy mixtures so frequently sold. Vein's Lightning Cough Cure is a scientific remedy, and has received endorsement from many eminent men." "What do you recommend it for ? " "Coughs, bronchitis, asthma, and influenza. It is a splendid remedy for whooping cough in children, and seldom fails to stop an ordinary coueh in one night ; it will subdue influenza in 24 hours. Daring the epidemic of influerza which raged throughout the northern and eastern portion of America in 1897, Veno'a Lightning Cough Cure was the chief remedy used. Ev-n physicians never hesitated to prescribe l.' "Do you recommend it for consump'‘on P " "In the first stages, yea, but not in the last. It nor- tame a preparation discovered in California by Dr. W P. Gibbons, and which was found to be a specific for bron- chitis and weak lungs. By curing these ailments con- sumption is prevented." Mr Veno then turned up a folio containing hundreds of testimonials, many of them speaking in the most flat- tering terms of the remedy. I admit, I never saw such a collection of testimonials in my life. "I will give you a coupie of honks of the Cough Cure," said Mr Veno, "take them home and when the occasion arises use them and speak of the remedy as you find it." div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL AND ITS AUDITORS.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL AND ITS AUDITORS.

The following comment on the dispute between the Warrington Town Council and izs auditors, which appeared in the leader colums of "The Accountant" on Saturday last, will probably be of interest to our readers. "The differences between the Warrington Town Council and its auditors, to which our attention has recently been directed, raise one or two impor- tant points. Exactly how these differences arose is, perhaps, not altogether clear from the informa- tion that 'snow before us, nor is it necessary that we should enquire closely into this point, seeing that it has little or no bearing upon the real ques- tion at issue. Suffice it to say that the auditors were Mr. Arthur Bennett, A.C.A. (who has held the post of Mayor's auditor for the past seven years), Mr. James Bolton, F.S.A.A. (vvtio has been one of the elective auditors for the past eleven years), and Mr. John Harrison, who does not appear to be a professional accountant. Two professionals out of three is considerably above the average in con- nection with the audit of municipal account, and there is, therefore, every reason to assume prima facie that the auditors were thoroughly well quali- fied to discharge their duties. These gentlemen examined the accounts for the year ended 31st March 1900, and issued their report thereon, uu .er idate of the 27th July 1900, as follows:
Warrington, 27th July 19n. To the Mayor. Aldermen. and Burgesses of the Borough of Virarringtm.

Mtn Sins,— BOROUGH AUDIT. We have pleasure in reporting that we have completed our audit of the accounts of the Corporation for the year ended 31st March 1900, including the accounts of Gas and Water Departments and Parr Hall. he duties of borough auditors, up to the time of our last report were limited, according to the best authorities, to the actual verification of accounts which had been aanctioned by the , various responsible committees. Their scope, however, has been extended by the subsoquent decision of the Court of Appeal. in Thomas v. The Corporation of Devon- port. Whereas Mr. Justice Phillimore considered the simple vouching of the receipts and payments the whole duty of the auditors. the Lord Chief Justice, in the Higher Court, says that they are bound to ascertain, amongst other things. wtether the payments are duly authorised and legal. We notice that certain expendi- ture in connection with the recent Borough Bill has been provided for out of the Walker Gift Fund, instead of being charged upon the rates. We are of opinion that 11 the manner in which the Middleton Scholarship his been dealt with is not legal, and that the interest from the bequest, instead of being accumulated, ought to ha,. a been at once applied to the purposes indicated by the will. We think It our duty to call attention to the large' amount which is annually expended upon deputations, and to the increasing disposition towards extravagance In this matter, and we notice that the Corporation sub- scribes to many voluntary associations and societies, and sends large deputations periodically to attend their meet- ings. The expenditure under both these heads wants carefully watching, and there are other items in winch a judicious economy might be practised with advantage. Faithfully yours, (Signed) ARTHUR BENNETT (Chartered Accountant). Mayor's Auditor. Joan HARBISON, JAMES BOLTON, F.S.A.A. Bleetive Auditors. _ .

This report, however, was not Pails-I'lW along with the Corporation's accounts in the usual way, and we understand that its contents were not made known until the meeting of the Town Council,which took place on the Bth January last, when the Chair- man of the Finance Committee defended the sup- pression of the report on the ground that its' publi- cation would not have been consistent with the dignity of the borough or helped to maintain its reputation.' It was also argued that the auditors had exceeded their duties, and that several of the statements contained in their report were incor- rect. It seems to us that, if the reputation of toe borough were likely to suffer by the publication of , the auditors' report, this would not of itself afford any justification for its suppression, even if such suppression could, in point of fact, be really effsc- tive. But naturally, all that could possibly be done was to delay the publication of the report, and no AT that it is issued after a lapse of six months,the very procedure adopted in order to keep it back has resulted in its receiving far greater publicity than it would ever have achieved in the ordinary course. It is clear, however, that even if the auditors had greatly exceeded theicduties, and even if all the statements contained in their report could be dis- proved, no justification, whatever would be afford- , ded tor the suppression of their report. The safe- guard afforded by an audit would be absolutely futile, if it were open to those whose accounts are being checked to suppress the result of the investi- gation. As to whether or not all the statements contain° 1 in the auditors' report can be proved up to the hilt, is a point with which we do not propose to concern ourselves here. The matter is doubtless of interest to the Town Council and to the ratepayers of War- rington; but, as we have already stated, even if the whole report were a tissue of fictions, no justifi- cation would be afforded for its suppression, and the point is, therefore, one that need not be dis- cussed in connection with the duties cf municipal auditors in general, or the treatment meted out to these auditors in particular. With regard to tha question as to whether the auditors exceeded their duties in reporting as they did, as Mr. Bennett pointed out, at the Council meeting al eady referred to, the present state of the law with regard to the matter •is unsatisfactory, Until quite recently the view was very generally held that the duties of elective auditors were limited to an examination of the Borough Treasurer's accounts, hut in the case of Thomas v. The Corporation of Devonport the late Lord Chief Justice expressed the opinion that an auditor's duties went much further thsn this, and until the law is amended or better defined it is (Mr. Bennett stated) the bounden duty of auditors to bring their bet abilities to bear upon the work that they have to do, while it would clearly not be safe for them to altsgether ignore the late Lord Russell's dictum with regard to the matter. The Mayor of Warrington has, it would appsar. some original views upon the subject. Be is reported to nave said that Lord Russell's remarks are "only applic- able to cases of illegality of an obvious nature'; and that it is not for elective auditors to set them- selves up as lawyers, and decide what is legal and what is illegal, but that if anything of an "ob- viously illegal character" should come under their notice, ills for them to bring the matter before the Committee. How an auditor is to judge as to whether or not certain transactions are even •• obviously " illegal without setting himself up as a lawyer to some extent is by no means clear ; but if it be any part at all of an auditor's duty to scrutinise trans- actions with a view to seeing whether or not they are duly authorised,it is quite clear that the auditor must accept no guide as to what is irregular and what is not, other than his own opinion. And, al- though it would be manifestly unreasonable to ex- pect auditors to have a thorough knowledge on points of law, and to hold them negligent if they failed to show themselves possessed of such know- ledge, iris equally clear that where they are bona- fide of opinion that certain transactions are ques- tionable it is their duty to call attention to them. Equally certain is it that an auditor has not dis- charged his duties by reporting to the very persons whom he is appointed to check. For an auditor's report to be made to the Committee alone would be to reduce the audit to a ridiculous farce, If the auditors have anything to say, it isessential that it should be said to the right people. The net outcome of the whole matter is that both 3fr. Bennett and Mr. Bolton have resigned their respective po,itions in disgust. Precisely why they should have thought it necessary to take this step Iwe cannot say. It seems to us that at a juncture like the present,it is especially important that audi- tors who are prepared to rep3rt independently should be appointed at Warrington, rather than ',editors who may be prepared to fall in with the Council's somewhat extraordinary view with regard to their duties. However,public attention has now been fully directed to the issue, and it will be the ratepayers' own fault if they do not know how to act when the next elections come round. "

The Right Hon. Ctmrls T Ritchie. the home seprptary wrote stating that he was commanded by the King to convey His Majesty's thanks for the expression of sym- pathy with His Majesty and the Royal. Family on the occasion of the lamented death of her late Majes
-- - - rANcugigE'S EXPRESSION OF . SYMPATHY AND LOY tr..TY.

_ The Chairman reported that he received a comm ~licat- ion from Lord Derby calling a meeting of the public representatives ot Lancashire to be held at Preston on the 12th February for the purpose of passing a resolution expressing their deep sorrow at the death of her late Majesty and also their loyal good wishes to Sing Edward VII. on his accession to the Throne. He (the chairman) thoughs he would be doing psrfectly right in attending the meeting on the Council's behalf and he had the pleasure of doing so. The meeting was a most impressive one and was very largely attended. They had a very lengthy address from the Earl of Derby,Lord Cross and several other gentlemen, and it was unani- mously decided to present an address to His Majesty. Mr Borr m proposed a vote of thanks to Mr Coiling- wood for representing the Council en such an important occasion. Their chairman would, he thought have been censured if he had not done so. Mr Emmett seconded the vote of thackq, and addsd that Mr Coiling wood would have neglected his duty if ha had not attended the meeting. The vote of thanks was unanimously passed. The Chairman, in acknowledging the compliment,said he was very plea& d to fulfil that duty.

div.head: NOTES ON -LIANIES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football. • [By " Ovalist."]
div.p: NOTES ON -LIANIES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football. • [By " Ovalist."]

Warrington are on the high road to fame and fortune, I for by surviving the opening round in the Northern Union Cup Competition they ensure themselves immun- ity from travelling until the semi-final is reached, providing that some club does not come to Wilderspool and conquer in the meantime. With the prospect of having Ileckmondwike, Leeds Parish Courch and Bradford as visitors, Warrington's hopes fioancially and otherwise are of the brightest, and both players and 1 supporters are in the seventh heaven of delight—per- haps the only heaven some of them will ever get in. I heard of a man the other day who said he thought heaven eould not passhlv be better than a good cigar and a drop of whiekey, but he was an easily-satisfied

It was a long journey that Warrington people took in order to see the team qualify themselves for the cup tourney. Leeds is well within the confines of the broad- acred shire, and when you journey there by the Great Central and Great Northern route you appreciate fully the value of the locomotive as an invention. It's nearly N miles over the line on which the Warrington crowd travelled, but it was the only way of getting there with any comfort. There are few railway companies which lay themselves out to accomodate excursionists as the Great Central people do, and we owe them our gratitude for transferring a thousand of us so conveniently from Warrington to Leeds. Two special trains were required, including no less than 15 saloons, which were raked up from all qoarters of the railway system to satisfy the demands of the plutocratic Warfingtonians.

One of the thins the ardent supporter was most hop- ing for was fine weather on this occlsion. Very vivid recollections exist of the terrible semi-final at Hudders- field when Warrington were swamped by the weather and the Batley Club conjointly. It is generally admitted 1 that Warrington do not shine in the mud, but for once in a way they rose superior to circumstances. The weather was almost as vile as it knows how to be in this dam—p climate and during the whole of the morning and most of the afternoon of Saturday it rained and blew in the most vicious manner. As is usual with Yorkshire grounds,that at Headingley is perched on the top of the hill, where the full fury of the blast is not wasted one iota. Consequently, at the time fur kicking cff everything was as bad as it could be. There was a regular gale in action and the playing field was for all the world like a swamp, with a few stray blades of grass peering nervously over the waste of waters. However, not believing very much in the efficacy of protests because its wet. Warrington played, and played, so well that they astanished everybody.

Saturday's perforrnatre was undoubtedly one of the finest in the history of the Warrington club when every- thing is considered. Leeds are a Yorkshire first division club and on their own ground might be expected to give any other club a warm time in a cop tie. Then the weather suited them, or at least they thought it would do prior to the match and they had hopes that the admittedly smarter club from Lincashire would be sent bsck de- feated. Nothing of the sort happened. Warrington lost the toss and faced the music—otherwise the gale— in the first half, and played with so much decerrninatiOn and skill that they got the better of tha Leeds" Loiners" and credited themselves with a try by Fish. who seemed in his iement on Saturday. Water is a fish's element, of con.yse, but as a rule John Fish of that ilk prefers dry land,wharein he is sensible. Leeds could not score or get near it and at half time were, to all intents and put - poses, beaten.

Warrington simply made hack; of the " loiners" defence in the second half and ran in no less than six trios, though two of thee., (by Fell and Htllam) were not allowed. The combination of the Lancashire lads was superb and the way they handled the wet ball partook more of jugglery than football. I never saw a club of good standing so completely non-plussed by their oppon- ente as were Leeds on Sa'urday, and, in addition,' never saw Warrington plat' so magnificently in every depart- ment. Fish got another try by jigging round Jagger in front of the goal, while Isherwood, B tte and Harris scored the others as the outcome of masterly combin Um. Fish also kicked three goals, and the home club's tale of woe at the fini3h was one of 21. points to nil.

On the winning side it is difficult to pick out indivi- duals who merited praise, for all did 80 Well and all seemed as imbued with one idea, that the team was 1 more like a perfect machina than anything else. The halfbacks cannot be overlooked, however, for their superb cmabination and inientitic play was the secret of Warrington's success. Both Bate and Duckworth played above themselvea " and the display of the latter, in particular, was marvellon.. He ran clean through the , Leeds backs time after time, thus making openings that the chrmquarters could not h-lp utilising, and in addi- tion ha tacklai Ilk a tiger. Fish and Lher cvsod were &No at tho op of choir form and infused a large amount of dasii iaio crii,ir play, while Dickenson and Harris more than held their own on th. right. The former cmply justified hie selection. Hallam ws the only player who disappointed, and even he could not be blamed for missing the hall as he did in the first half when the con- ditions were so much against him. The fact that we have got into the bible of expecting Hallam to miss nothing had probably something to do with our disap- pointment. He certainly gave his side some anxious moments. The Warrington forwards worked finely and were much superior to a somewhat heavier, set opposed to them. The winning team, altogether, gave a dis-,lay which promises very well indeed for future cup con- tests. OLD FALSE TEETH BOUGHT:

div.head: LOCAL PARISH ELECTIONS.
div.p: LOCAL PARISH ELEC- TIONS.
A Poll Demanded at Padgate and Helsby.

Monday evening witnessed the holding of the annual parish meetings in connection with the Pariah Councils in this district. The proceedings were of more than usual interest as the parishioners had the opportunity of electing their representa- tives on the Parish Councils for the ensuing three years. Most of the meetings passed off very quietly, and at only two places—Padgae and He'shy—was a poll demanded. A peculiar incident occurred at liorlev, where the parish meeting refused to nomi- nate any candidates, the general opinion of the village being they preferred to revert back to the the system of vestry me stings once a year. Natur- ally this cannot be done, and the result will be that old retiring councillors will have to serve :

div.head: TREATMENT OF NIGHTSOIL.
div.p: THE TREATMENT OF NIGHTSOIL.

In answer to Mr Tonge, Mr Balton stated that he htd had the matter of the fres trn int of the nightsoil before the Council for three months, and he could give an assurance that the system adopted at Penketh and other places would before long be used in Sankey.

THE SCHOOL MARL) RATE. -7Mr Thompson said that Aeveral ratepayers would like to know the reason of the very heavy rate for School Board purposes. They were paving in Sankey some- thing like 7.1 in the round for School Board purnoses,and they would be glad to be informed as to how thtl money was spent. Mr Halton replied that it had been the endeavour of the members ever since he bad been elected to keen the rates down, and they were at the present time in a position to say that there would be a reduction foe the next financial half-year. He did not think the schools could be worked more economically than they were. The repayment of the loan kept the rates tip. Re thought before long,hewever,they would be in a position to reduce the rates considerably. The Chairman said that when he took the position of schoolmaster 15 years ago the rate was is. At the present time it was between 61 and 7.1. During the last ten years the rate for the school itself had not exceeded 21. It had rarely exceeded a penny for school purposes. During two of those years the school had not only neer the rates nothing but had actually plod back a balance from the grant. (Hear, hear.) Last year with a much less average than the previous year they earned more grant. The amount of money 'earned per child was larger thanithat in any school in Warrington with the ex caption, he believel, of one school. (Hear, hear.) The average per head wag 22i 61 for the whole school. The grant earned wag £2T4, and that was done with the or- dinary staff. Before long they would be compelled by the insprctor to provide more staff. The greater the in- crease IR the number of children the more money the school earned. If there was an increase of 30 children £45 was earned, and from that they could pay an as- sistat.t £4O and be £5 to the good. The more enlidren the better for the school and consequently the rates There was accommodation for another 100 children. _
Mr, Thompson asked how long it would be before the loan was paid off. Ttr, Coairman said the money was borrowed in 1884. It WAS a 30 year' loan.

TILE CONDITION OF MR ROADS. Mr A Birch drew attention to whit he described /19 the unsatisfactory condition of the road between Sankey Bridges and the lan-ends. The road, he said, was not kept as it used to be.

Mr Halton said the footway along that road would never be in good condition as long as the embankment remained above to drain the field into the road. The position was rather an unfortunate one. The authorities were contemplating cindering the footpath between Sankey Bridges and Mr Jeans's property. He would bring the matter before the next Council meeting. He might say that there was a greater expenditure on Great Sankey than any o'her parish of the rural district. The main roads of the district were maintained by the County Council.
Other matters were discussed, and a vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the meeting.
THE HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT. DR SEPEETON'S STATEMENT CHALLENGED.

Mr Thompson drew attention to a remark made at the last meeting of the Rural District Council by the filedical Officer, Dr Sephton. The matter of the health of the district was brought up, and Dr Smhton said "he would not say Penketh, but the sub-registration d'striet of Sankey, was always in an unhealthy condition." H (Mr Thompson) thr,ught that statement ought not to go unchallenged. (Hear, hear.) He thought Sankey was about as healthy a district as any in the country. It was most serious for the property owners in the district that a gentleman should get up at a meeting of a public body and make such a statement. It should not pass unchallenged. He hoped the Press would refer to the matter and clear Sankey of such a charge. Mr Halton said that when the statement was made h asked the Medical Officer whether Buttonwood was not Included in the sub-registration district, and was told that it was. As a matter of fact not much reliance could be placed on the statement, because when some time ago Dr Sephton made a report in conjunction with Dr Sergeant, the county medical officer' to the Council regarding the proposed site at Sankey for the small-pox hoipital, ho said there was not a more healthy part in the whole district of the Council. How could they account for two such directly opposite statements ? He (Mr Halton) simply ignored the statement at the last 'meeting: Li was his intention however, since the matter had appeared in the Press, to- write challenging Dr Sephton to make good the state meet. Since the matter had been brought forward now that was unrxecsiary, but he should certainly challenge the doctor at the next meeting of the Council upon the two statements which had been made.

The Chairman said it --should --certainly be decided whether the doctor was right or not, because the qunp- tion wag one of vital importance. Re personally that Sankey was the second highest diztrict on that side of the river, and had the lowest death rate.
On the motion of ir Ilalt,n, sen'onciediw Mr Fulton Smith, a vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman.

THE DI;TRICT COUNCIL AND THE PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.

Mr Lord : II it a fact that four members are nomin- ated and elected by the District Council to sit upon our Parochial Committee—to have a vote on all the lousiness —who are neither ratepayers nor residents ? Tao Clerk : That is a fart, an i there is no remedy. Mr. Pemberton : There is a remedy ; it ought to be remedied by the District Council who ought to object to such a procfeding. S;ockton Reath is the only district in the Runcorn Council's area which has outside repre- sentatives on the Parochial Committee. I fail to see why three other district cluncillors should come out of their districts to have a voice in the spending of our maney. (Hear, hear.) A member asked for the attendances and they were read. Mr. Lord: I think we might move a vote of thanks to them. (Laughter.)
MR. ENG-LAND-PREFERS AN 17RBANATITIIORITY.

Mr. England contended that a Parish Coancil was not suitable for the requirements of a:place like Stockton Beath. Many of them bad been alive to that fact for many years. Ho had held to the opinion for a consider- able time that they were a set of noodles to put up with a form of government like the present one By being connected with the Ruicorn Rural District Council they were placed under a great disadvantage ; in fact they were suffering in pocket and health. Under the Agricultural Rates Acts, the farmers and others only paid half the rates whilst Stockton Heath residents had to pay the whole of the rates. The rates instead of be- coming lees, were becoming higher, and yet they obtained no corresponding advantage. 'ale only adds- tins for the last four years had been a few lamps, although several hundred housea had been put up. A parish council for a district like this was a complete farce. It only suited two sections of the community— property owners and builders. (Laughter.) A criticism was passed upon the manner in which certain houses were built, and th 3 speaker also contended that houses which ought to be pulled down were allowed to remain. He strongly advocated the formation of a svarate urban authority for Stockton heath, and pointed out that far' less impottant places had an urban authority of their own. _ . _

_ Mr. Pembr_.rtou quite agreed with Mr. England that Stockton ,Heath should have a batter form of local government, but the sweeping assertions he had made about the builders were quite out of order. (L tughter.) He did not say "some builders " but " all builders." (nenewed laughter.) Their Surveyor had plenty of time at his disposal, and if there was any building that was not what it ought to be he was to blame. They could not carry out the improvements in the footpaths and roads because the District Council would not spend the necessary money.

RUNCORN UNION.-CONTRACTS FOR PRO- VISIONS AND SUPPLIES FOR THI4 HALF-YRAR ENDING OCTOBER iTII. 1901. The GUARDIA.NS of the Poor of the RUNCORN UNION are desirous of receiving TENDERS from parties willing to CONTRACT for the supply of New Milk, Buttermilk, Fresh Rutter. and Fresh Eggs (for Twelve Months), Flour, Oat- Meal, Groceries, Peas, Cheese, and Salt Butter ; Cod Liver and Paraffin Oil; Quinine ; Good Thief. to consist of vein pieces intact and Fiat Ribs with Bone, one round weekly not Lo exceed 251b5.. and 50lbs. per week of the Best Butcher's 72at for the Officer!, and sides of Mutton ; Bread, Home- -5d Bacon, P dittoes, Wheat Straw; Drapery, and tilething ; Men n Women's, Boys' and Girls' Shoes of various then, as per samples to be seen at the Workhouse, Dutton, ',.t,nd shoe Mending; House Coal (Colliery to be named) ; wood Heal Coffins. specifying size. and including plate, with name, age, and death, to be delivered in the Union when and Where required ; Coke ; Carting at per mile; Funerals at per Funeral. Parties Tendering for the supply of the above-mentioned Goods will be required to deliver the same at the Workhouse, free rt cost to the Guardians, how and when required. Tenders to be accompanied with samples (except Drapery Goods) as far as practicable. The Guardians do not bind themselves to accept the Lowest or any tender. Persons desirous Of tendering mu!t apply by letter to my office, in RatlCOna. for a printed Form of Tender (and none other can be entertained), where a Schedule of the various articles required and further particulars my be obtained. Sealed Tenders addressed to the Guardians,to be forwarded to the Clerks Office. Runcorn, on or before Monday, the 25th March 1901, endorsed '• Tender for The Tenders will be opened and considered at a Meeting Of the Guardians to be held in the Boardroom, Dutton, on the 26th dar of March, 1931, at 12 45 p.m. Parties whose tenders are accepted must enter into a written contract, and be prepared to enter into a Bond with two Sureties, if reqiiired by the Guardians By order of the Board. GEO. F. ASHTON. Clerk to the Guardians. Runcorn, lit March, 1931.

-- ELECT lON OF GUAR IH ANS.—TO THE RUICTORS OF ST, AUSTIN'S No, 2 WARD. Lams AND GENTLEMEN. Having been asked to become a Ca" didate for this Ward and received the promise of support from many friends and leading residents, I have very great pleasure in offer- ing my services. Knowing the needs and conddion of the Ward as I do, and having a large business connection in it which r.quires regular and personal attention,l am in a position to look alter your interests to be very best advantage. If elected, my (fforts on the Board would be directed to "economy. 'conjoined with efficiency," while the Bmbazon Scheme, and the division of the inmates for the Special treatment of the weak and deserving, would have zny sympathetic support. Being a trades 17, ionist, and affiliated with the Trade And Labour Council, I should Support the insertion of the fair wages clause in all contracts entered into with the Board. Either myself:or friends Will have the pleasure of wait- ing upon you prior to the &anion. Trusting to have your hearty co-operation, and to be favoured with your votes. I remain. Yours Sincerely, RICHARD AmissoN. . Whits-street, Warring^ on.

ELECTION OF GUARDIANS, 1931. TO THE ELECTORS OF ST. AUSTIN'S No. 2 WARD: , LAMES AN'D GENTLEMEN, My term of office having nearly expired. I once more offer my services as a Candidate for the position of Guardian for this Ward. I have been a member of the Board of Guardians for the last three years, and during the time named, I have attended nearly every Board and Committee meeting. which has been held. As a member of the Relief Committee I have always strongly advocated and supported in giving adequate relief to the cases which have come before us, to treat the deserving poor in such a manner as would help them to tide over their temporary difficulties and prevent their homes being broken up, and if you again honour me. with your confidence, I can assure you that no efforts of mine will be wanting to f ulfil the duties of the positbn. lam, yore faithfully, THOMAS H. ASHCROFT. 135. Sankey-street. Warrington. March let, 1901.

The following are the articles for which TENDERS are required : Groceries and Provisions iihoes, Clogs and Slippers Beef and Mutton Glazing Joints for Officers Brushes Flour and Irish pin head meal Coffins Loaves and Bread Best Oakum rope for picking Straw and Potatoes Best Penmaentnavvr Stone Drapery &c, for breaking purposes ' Cord and Twill Leather Coal, Slack. and Gas Coke Samples of any of the above may be seen on application to the Master of the Workhouse.
